Under the premise that the ground state is known and that its spatial pattern is smooth, we derive a lower bound for the generalization error in terms of potential parameters of the neural network and the complexity of the ground state's support. Notably, our findings do not rely on any statistical assumption regarding the sample data, and we provide guidance on the selection of the neural network's hyperparameters. Furthermore, we conduct a series of numerical experiments to verify our theoretical results. The methods employed in this study are inspired by recent research on the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for solving partial differential equations. The key ideas and techniques involved are reviewed, and it is demonstrated that the analysis can be applied to a wide range of equations, including the Shrödinger, Helmholtz, and Navier-Stokes equations. Additionally, we derive an upper bound for the generalization error, and our numerical results are consistent with the theoretical findings. The methods developed in this study are expected to be valuable for addressing various quantum engineering challenges. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers studied the properties of hexagonal (H2) and cubic (H3) ices at high pressure and found that, within a certain pressure range, these ices exhibit a unique behavior. Below a specific temperature, and at pressures between 0.5 and 0.6 of the critical value, these ices spontaneously form smaller, ordered areas. As the temperature rises, these ordered areas grow, and at the critical pressure, the ice transitions into a single, crystalline phase. Furthermore, by mimicking an ice cube's freezing process and examining its structural state, the researchers discovered that, even at temperatures close to its final freezing point, this ice exhibits partial ordering and may contain small, crystalline domains. This partial ordering may contribute to the unusual appearance of the ice's surface and its slower cooling curve. It could also potentially be seen under an electron microscope due to the distinct interaction between the ice and certain materials. However, previous attempts to directly observe these ordered regions using such microscopes have yielded inconsistent results, which can now be explained by our computer simulation's findings, suggesting that, under normal conditions, the transition to a crystalline phase is incomplete and the ice remains partially disordered. As a result, the transition from an amorphous to a crystalline state is not complete, which could have significant implications for various scientific fields and understanding of the ice's behavior.  Finally, based on these findings, the researchers suggest a possible way to directly observe the ordered regions that form under high pressure at low temperatures by manipulating the conditions to which certain substances are exposed. This research could potentially lead to significant advances in various scientific fields, including how the transition from an amorphous to a crystalline state occurs and what factors influence it.  In addition, the findings could have significant implications for space-related scientific fields, such as Mars, due to the low temperatures and pressure on the planet's surface. Our study focuses on the Isabelle Archive's directory structure and formal proofs hierarchy, and we investigate the relationships between them. Superconducting qubit performance is constrained by dielectric loss. Experimental evidence sets upper limits on dielectric loss tangents, approximately $100$ parts-per-billion, however this has yet to be directly observed. We've developed a dielectric loss measurement technique based on the atomic interaction between the dielectric and helium-3 atoms in the hyperpolarized liquid state. By applying magnetic field gradients to separate the spins of the dielectric and sample, the dielectric loss can be directly measured by its impact on nuclear spin relaxation. We've used this technique to assess $8.7$ parts-per-billion dielectric loss tangents in sapphire cylinders at frequencies of approximately $8$ gigahertz, demonstrating the effectiveness of the method. The development of pattern extraction algorithms helps gain valuable insights into ever-growing datasets by translating recurring data features into simplified representations. However, as dataset volumes and complexities increase, the number of discovered patterns grows exponentially, overwhelming analysts with an extensive result space. Most existing algorithms and visualization methods struggle to accommodate such large sets of patterns. To address this issue, we have created a visual analysis framework that facilitates in-depth exploration of pattern catalogs by allowing users to discover patterns visually. By translating surface pattern densities into volume-based representations, our visuualization method offers different levels of abstraction that help users distinguish between volumetric data distributions and surface-only pattern representations. Furthermore, users can create interactive visualizations to analyze patterns that cannot be discovered manually. We have evaluated our approach's efficacy with multiple example use cases and through an expert review that involved domain-specific aircraft black box data analysis. All expert review experiments have been made accessible through an online demo platform. Our method presents a range of simplification and abstraction options that make it possible to create a volume-based representation of pattern catalogs even on 3D time-varying data sets. To date, there are few algorithms available that can create a coherent and complete representation of detected patterns. We have extended the capabilities of the Coocurceo algorithm, initially developed for static datasets, to accommodate time-varying data sets. By applying in-depth analysis and the systematic evaluation of different variants, we have refined the Coocurceo algorithm's output, providing users with a set of derived invariants that aid in pattern extraction and visualization. Ultimately, the results of our method's evaluation confirm that it can be efficiently applied to various use cases, and our method allows users to create a volume-based representation of discovered patterns. Our approach consists of different levels of abstraction and aggregation, and our method outperforms basic visual analysis methods due to its ability to accurately accommodate large sets of patterns. All of our method's evaluation experiments have been made accessible through an online demo platform that can be accessed at the following link: https://pattern-analysis.app. Additionally, the outcome of our expert review has received the following awards: - The Star Prize at the 2022 IJCBS Awards for Outstanding Contributions to the Field of Computer Engineering. - The Best Paper Award at the 2022 IEEE Symposium on Visual and Visual Analytics. All of the awards received by our method have been acknowledged by leading experts in the field of computer engineering. Ultimately, the results of our expert review confirm that our method can be efficiently applied to visual analysis of big data.

Building on Sodemann and Fu's theory of the nonlinear Hall effect established in 2015, 
a semiclassical framework where it arises from Bloch electrons' anomalous velocity as a geometric property,
a broader theory is presented, encompassing correlated and disordered systems. 
Within this theory, a generally consistent method is presented to calculate both the linear and nonlinear Hall conductivity,
with a special focus on a two-dimensional system where Anderson localization occurs.
Results show that when a mean field potential is applied, correlation between occupied states can be introduced,
without explicitly interacting with the system's dynamics.
This potential's influence vanishes in well-localized, weakly interacting situations,
allowing for a separation of effects caused by disorder and interaction,
which are reminiscent of Anderson's theory of localization.
Additionally, a nonlinear Hall conductivity is present in scenarios with weak disorder and interaction,
even when symmetrical, correlated hoppings are involved.
Nonlinear Hall effects are diminished by disorder in clean situations but could serve as an indicator for semi-clean conditions.
Analysis on a 2D lattice indicates that nonlinear Hall conductivity can be generated in localized, weakly interacting systems,
where interactions between anisotropic, correlated bands lead to a non-zero nonlinear Hall conductivity,
along with a study of linear Hall conductivity within the regime of a Wigner lattice formed under extreme correlation.
All calculations presented here align with the original semiclassical, geometric framework of the nonlinear Hall effect. 
This framework is independent of band structure or other materials-based factors,
which are not relevant in the given theoretical context,
therefore enabling a generally consistent approach to analyze both the linear and nonlinear Hall conductivity. 
This method can be applied to a broader category of materials, including quantum spin Hall candidates and topological insulators. 
It is anticipated that these results will be confirmed experimentally through the use of a specific pump-probe experiment designed to quantify the nonlinear Hall effect. 
This experiment is discussed in the companion article.

In 2002, Biss researched a type of fibration known as the rigid fibration (initially called the rigid covering fibration), exhibiting properties akin to covering spaces. This study establishes a connection between general topological spaces and their corresponding rigid fibrations. This relationship enables a commutative diagram involving homotopy groups and quasitopological homotopy groups, resulting in an exact sequence. This study also demonstrates that another type of fibration, the total spaces of Postnikov structures, also yields an analogous diagram and exact sequence. The core of topological band theory, Bloch's theorem, is a fundamental concept in quantum materials research. Nevertheless, it is disrupted by perpendicular magnetic fields, rendering the study of strong magnetic flux challenging for topological systems. The advent of moiré materials brings this challenge to life, prompting researchers to explore its solution. This research investigates twisted bilayer graphene under a $2\pi$ flux, revealing a reentrant flat band that persists across all spin channels. The findings are further validated by computational models for short-range hopping and tight-binding simulations. Additionally, this study examines the emergence of Chern bands under these conditions. The discovery of a reentrant flat band provides valuable insights into moiré materials under magnetic flux and has significant implications for low-universal flux quantum Hall research in these systems. Furthermore, this study contributes to our understanding of magnetic Bloch theorem in systems with strong magnetic fields. The reentrant flat bands could facilitate the creation of topological flat bands by stacking two moiré semiconductors in an ABA pattern. The absence of a band touching that persists across all spin channels might limit the use of twisted moiré materials for low-flux quantum Hall effect research. Finally, this study explores the potential of twisted bilayer graphene under a $2\pi$ flux as a platform for Fermi surface topological flat bands. In this study, the calculation of Gromov-Wasserstein distance under the constraints of local differential privacy is explored, leading to the development of a universally applicable method for comparing distributed graph data while maintaining confidentiality. The proposed approach involves the initial application of differential privacy to transform sensitive graph data, the subsequent application of Gromov-Wasserstein distance in a manner that respects confidentiality, and a final examination of its accuracy and effectiveness. The integration of local differential privacy into our analysis yields a metric system for graph data that's both accurate and confidential. Additionally, our method successfully generalizes to images captured under new conditions, including images with varying exposure and noise. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends traditional group generators to account for a specific order in which elements are multiplied together. It is established that any finite Coxeter group of B-type can be represented as a product of consecutive transpositions within a predetermined framework for OGS representations. Furthermore, the group Bn can be expressed in two distinct OGS forms, corresponding to sequences generated by even-lengthed transpositions or sequences generated by sequences of two transpositions. OGPs (ordered generating power sequences) serve as a comprehensive classification of group representations, distinct from traditional presentations which prioritize minimal length representations. However, OGPs are neither exhaustive nor exclusive, with multiple OGPs possible for the same group representation. OGPs are considered equivalent if one can be derived from the other through a finite number of operations preserving the group's structure and a set length limit. OGPs can be used to categorize a subset of symmetric groups, prioritizing shorter sequences, with the goal of demonstrating that any given OGP for Sn can serve as a representation for some finite Coxeter group of B-type, a claim which remains unproven at the time of writing. OGPs are also applied to infinite groups within the B-type family, including direct limit groups and their potential application in combinatorics, particularly in analyzing OGP relationships between permutation groups and their invariants. Lastly, the l2 automorphism problem for the groups Qn (quaternion groups) serves as an example of ongoing research seeking a direct proof that any given OGP for a finite group representation can serve as a representation for some B-type Coxeter group. If successful, this proof would imply every OGP for a finite group representation is equivalent to an OGP representing a Coxeter group of T-type (also referred to as a reflection group). Currently, this proof remains unprovable due to the inherent limitations of finite group representation theory. However, the possibility of finding a direct proof or proving its impossibility holds significant value in the ongoing study of fundamental group theory. As a result, further research is necessary to validate the possibility of representing any given OGP for a finite group representation through a Coxeter group of B-type. Our research shows that lattice calculations can be used to derive transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions, such as gluon TMDs, by combining constraints from lattice simulations and soft factor calculations. This is achieved through large-momentum effective theory, which enables the construction of TMDs with arbitrary momentum scale. By taking into account next-to-leading-order corrections from lattice calculations and next-to-leading-log corrections from renormalization and evolution processes, we can obtain the final TMDs in the desired scale. This work marks an important step towards understanding the partonic structure of protons at high energies. Although our discussion focuses on gluon TMDs, the techniques can be applied to analyze other parton species. Our findings are expected to contribute significantly to the ongoing efforts of extracting TMDs from experimental data and constructing custom-made TMDs for specific analyses. Moreover, our work lays the foundation for future investigations of various physics topics, including the partonic structure of heavy quark systems, nucleon-nucleon collisions, quark-gluon separation, and exotic hadrons. In the context of ultra-peripheral collisions between heavy ions, the photon-photon interaction leads to the creation of $e^+e^-$ pairs in the vicinity of heavy nuclei. When these electrons and positrons have low transverse momenta, they are easily captured by the nuclei, resulting in the electrons and positrons (e/e) accelerating inside the nuclei' electric fields. As a consequence, the nuclei' bremsstrahlung radiation produces additional e/e pairs, and this process is accompanied by a distinct emission of x-rays. Notably, the capture of e/e pairs is an example of photon-electron interaction, while the x-ray emission is a result of electromagnetic interaction between electrons and the nuclei. Our analysis demonstrates that the electromagnetic interaction's effect on e/e production is comparable to the photons' contribution in ultra-peripheral collisions. Furthermore, the analysis presents a detailed calculation of e/e production and x-ray emission in ultra-peripheral collisions between lead nuclei at the Large Hadron Collider. The calculation takes into account both the radial electric field of the lead nuclei and the effects of relativistic electrons and positrons on the lead nuclei. The study finds that the electromagnetic interaction's impact on e/e production at transverse momenta less than 100 MeV/c is significantly greater than the photons' effect, accounting for approximately 80% of e/e production. Moreover, the production of this e/e pairs leads to an additional production of e/e pairs at transverse momenta larger than 400 MeV/c of about 0.2 per nucleon-pair per barn, which is comparable to a photon-induced process. The study also presents a distinct spectrum of x-ray photons that result from the e/e pairs' creation, with a peak intensity of approximately 10^7 erg/s at an energy of 17 MeV and a maximum yield of about 0.2 per nucleon-pair per barn. The analysis further reveals that the electromagnetic interaction's effect on e/e production at momenta less than 100 MeV/c at the Large Hadron Collider is expected to be approximately 2600 per barn, with a yield of about 0.2 per nucleon-pair per barn for the production of additional e/e pairs at momenta larger than 400 MeV/c. Tagging algorithms serve as essential tools for analyzing top-quark events, but they face challenges in high-energy environments. Previous studies have shown that machine learning techniques can improve top tagging, particularly in complex collision data. This research leverages boosted top tagging algorithms to enhance current methods and applies a novel interpretation technique using Shapley values to analyze the underlying components of the algorithms' performance. By evaluating the success of three boosted top tagging algorithms, we find that Shapley values can validate the advantages of boosted algorithms over traditional ones and reveal how Shapley values can serve as a performance metric for complex machine learning systems. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of measuring Shapley values directly from the algorithm's output during analysis phase. Overall, our study contributes to the advancement of top tagging and sheds light on the performance of machine learning algorithms. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates that Shapley values offer a universal way to evaluate the contributions of individual features or groups of features in complex machine learning systems. Finally, our study provides guidelines on the use of Shapley values as reliable and fair performance metrics for collaborative machine learning algorithms. Our investigation covers seven coadding methods: mean, median, and five variants of the Laplacian pyramid. Analyzing simulated data, we conclude that the nature of the input images and noise distribution greatly impact the accuracy of photometry and kernel calculations. Among the coadding algorithms, the mean performs best in photometry, whereas the median is superior for kernel calculations. According to our findings, the Laplacian pyramid methods fall in between these two in terms of kernel accuracy. Further, we discover that using a small number of high-weighted images can produce results comparable to the median algorithm, potentially leading to new methodologies to analyze space-based images. Our work also explores the limitations of existing coadding algorithms when dealing with unevenly sampled, time-resolved space data. Lastly, we highlight areas of application where the variation in PSFs between images might be advantageous, potentially allowing for enhanced analysis of such data in separate channels. Based on these insights, we propose new approaches for analyzing unevenly sampled, time-resolved space data, with the ultimate goal of making these methodologies accessible to the space-based astronomy community. In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm. We demonstrate that the solution's maximum norm grows at most quadratically with time, provided the initial conditions' maximum norm is sufficiently limited. Notably, this quadractic growth can mirror the behavior seen in the case of non-periodic but low-debye initial conditions. Further, we demonstrate that the solution's $C^{0, \gamma}$-norm maximum, associated with some $0<\gamma<1$, grows at most linearly with time, assuming the initial conditions' $\|u_0\|_{C^{0, \gamma}}$ is sufficiently limited. Conversely, increasing $\gamma$ results in quadratically growing $C^{0, \gamma}$-norm estimates. Interestingly, these quadratically growing estimates are shown to be intrinsic, much like the behavior seen in shearing motion models. It's also observed that increasing $\gamma$ essentially amounts to imposing additional restrictions on the velocity field's support. Moreover, we derive a Serrin-type condition for the Navier-Stokes equations' non-blown-up solutions, under periodic initial conditions and these specific estimates. Lastly, we show that our quadratically growing estimates for the periodic initial conditions' solutions align with the estimates obtained for non-periodic yet low-debye initial conditions. In particular, we prove that increasing $\gamma$ essentially amounts to imposing a stricter maximum norm restriction on the initial velocity field $u_0$. The obtained estimates represent improved, more refined estimates of the solution's quadratically growing $C^{0, \gamma}$-norm, applicable to the Navier-Stokes equations' Cauchy problem with periodic initial conditions and smooth periodic initial conditions. Interestingly, these refined quadratically growing estimates are unattainable via non-periodic yet low-debye initial conditions. Ultimately, we believe these results will contribute meaningfully to the analytical estimates of the solution's quadratically growing $C^{0, \gamma}$-norm for the Navier-Stokes equations' Cauchy problem under periodic initial conditions. Moreover, XLNet's effectiveness in modeling long-range dependencies is demonstrated through successful analysis on the NLPBenchmark, and it even surpasses the current best model in named entity recognition on the CoNLL-2003 dataset. This specific environment generates an accelerated, oscillating drag that facilitates neuronal activity and sensory perception in the optic lobes and central nervous system of the specimen. In-line with theoretical predictions from fluid dynamics, the specimen's center of mass moves at a speed determined by the average of fast and slow oscillating speeds. The difference between these speeds is directly linked to the magnitude of the oscillating drag. Additionally, our research supported the hypothesis that the optic lobes play a crucial role in the timing of the fast and slow phases of surface swimming, consistent with previous studies demonstrating related physiological processes. The findings of our study are also supported by the observations of another species that engages in a different form of surface swimming. The implications of our research suggest that the optimal speed of surface swimming in animals that use this method for movement may be difficult to predict due to the complex nature of the interaction between their bodies and the surrounding water. This framework can be applied universally, regardless of the species or structure, to make accurate predictions about the surface swimming speeds of animals based on their body size and movement patterns. Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current research has sought to automatically enhance taxonomies by learning concept representations in Euclidean space. However, the natural geometric structure of taxonomies aligns better with hyperbolic properties, making this space more suitable for representation. We propose HyperExpan, an algorithm that preserves the hierarchical structure of a taxonomy within a more expressive hyperbolic embedding space. It employs graph neural networks to capture relationships and characterizes profile information of concepts for accurate prediction during training. HyperExpan surpasses the performance of baseline models that utilize Euclidean space representation learning and achieves state-of-the-art results in taxonomy expansion benchmarks. The project's code and pre-trained models are publicly available.

Molecular systems' accuracy depends on accounting for non-covalent interactions. In this study, we analyze the electrostatic component of non-covalent interactions by evaluating the impact of external electric fields on the interaction energy between molecular pairs using ab-initio methods. We utilize a grid-based approach to estimate electrostatic potentials, thus obtaining variational potential energy components that can be compared with perturbation theory predictions. We analyze non-covalent interactions in charged and neutral pairs, focusing on the S66 dataset of 20 molecular dimers. We find that interactions involving dimers with significant permanent electric dipole moments are highly sensitive to external electric fields, with energy changes of up to 50kJ/mol in strong fields. In contrast, neutral pairs and dimers with internal charge balance exhibit minimal variation in interaction energy under external electric fields, averaging less than 0.1kJ/mol. We observe that the counter-intuitive behavior of charged red-shifted dimers in external electric fields is a general phenomenon that persists at higher electric field levels. We provide approximate relationships for predicting interaction energy changes at high electric field levels. We analyze the energy density of states to determine the underlying microscopic origin of the counter-intuitive behavior of charged red-shifted dimers. We find that the counter-intuitive behavior is a result of a balance between the kinetic energy of electrons in low-energy states and the potential energy of electrons in high-energy states. The latter is a result of the alignment of molecular dipoles induced by external electric fields. We discuss the potential implications of the observed behavior for molecular design. We conclude that neutral molecular pairs are ideal candidates for research into non-covalent interactions in external electric fields, given their stability and simplicity in comparison with charged systems. Moreover, the potential energy density of states provides valuable insight into the underlying microscopic balance between electron kinetic and potential energies. In light of the observed counter-intuitive behavior, it is recommended that neutral molecular dimers be used to design molecules that can withstand external electric fields, while charged systems may be suitable for applications where the counter-intuitive behavior is beneficial. Specifically, it is suggested that the interaction between a hydrogen atom and a molecular anion (in the water-dimethylether molecule) be used to design molecules that can withstand external electric fields. The proposed design suggestions open up new avenues for molecular design, where the proposed designs could be verified experimentally in the future. The probability of reaching two final states at a given time is calculated based on the current state and the transition probabilities. In this research, an attempt has been made to understand how the Casimir effect, caused by the zero-point fluctuations of electromagnetic waves, influences the thermodynamics of a blackbody. It has been attempted to establish a connection between the Casimir pressure's effect on a blackbody's surface area and the changes in its entropy and heat characteristics. However, the investigation found that maintaining consistency with the laws of thermodynamics proves to be a difficult task. Consequently, the research only considered systems where the Casimir effect introduces a change in energy that mirrors a blackbody's black-body radiation energy, thus setting its temperature to absolute zero. Under this condition, it was observed that the heat characteristics display the expected linear dependence on two distinct Casimir temperatures, one governing the system's entropy and the other governing its heat. Interestingly, when the Casimir effect is insufficient (large coupling constant, low temperature), the system's behavior converges to that of a traditional blackbody. Conversely, as the coupling constant varies from strong to weak, the system's behavior converges to a scenario in which two separate heat streams merge into a single uniform flow. Furthermore, when the system's temperatures become distinct, the system's thermodynamic properties appear to be rendered invariant. This significant finding implies that the Casimir effect's influence on a blackbody's thermodynamics appears to vanish when the system's temperatures become separate entities. Consequently, this property may serve as an indicator to detect the presence of the Casimir effect in a blackbody's thermodynamics. Lastly, the research explored the implications of quantum mechanics on a blackbody's surface, potentially introducing novel forms of entropy. While this possibility cannot be dismissed, the investigation found that such surface-related entropy is negligible in comparison to the blackbody's radiation entropy. Consequently, this surface-related entropy may be dismissed as a separate entity, thus preserving the traditional understanding of blackbody thermodynamics. Nonetheless, the research acknowledges the possibility of incorporating such surface-related entropy into a broader formulation of blackbody thermodynamics. Furthermore, the research concludes by acknowledging that incorporating the Casimir effect into a blackbody's thermodynamics through the method outlined in this investigation presents a challenging endeavor. Nonetheless, the research is offered as an initial attempt to explore this topic, in the hope that it may serve as a starting point for future investigations. Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships identified between these locations. Our proposed framework uses prior distributions conditioned on previous locations to measure and limit the likelihood of detecting actual traces given an individual's true location history. Our theoretical analysis confirms that our approach achieves the highest possible trace privacy guarantee compared to other methods. Additionally, our approach can be integrated into any privacy technique to enhance its performance, particularly in scenarios involving inter-session privacy. The results of our experiments align with our findings, highlighting the need for our proposed framework in protecting users' location histories. The analysis and evaluation code will be made accessible via GitHub. 

Despite the substantial achievements of our analysis and evaluation, there are distinct limitations to consider. Firstly, the applicability of our framework depends on the feasibility and cost of learning the HPDP for an individual's location history, which may not always be possible. Secondly, our framework assumes a common HPDP model for a given application, which may not reflect diverse models such as those influenced by roadmaps or social relationships in reality. Finally, our framework is not capable of addressing indirect privacy risks related to potential exposure to location-based services, not considered within this research. 

In summary, our analysis and evaluation confirm that our framework generates the optimal HPDP guarantee when protecting users' location histories and reveal significant performance limitations associated with previous techniques to be addressed.

A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves a pivotal role in lidar-based SLAM systems through the identification of recurring loops. The presented research introduces the NDT-Transformer approach, enabling real-time, large-scale place recognition using 3D point clouds. The methodology utilizes the 3D Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation to summarize dense point clouds into geometrical shape descriptions via probabilistic distributions. Subsequently, the novel NDT-Transformer network processes a set of 3D NDT cell representations to learn global descriptors enriched with both geometrical and contextual data. The final step entails descriptor matching via a query-database to pinpoint locations within pre-mapped areas. The proposed method, evaluated across the well-established KITTI and Stanford datasets, surpasses the existing benchmarks by extension. Moreover, an in-depth examination of the method's real-time performance from both offline and online processing perspectives in terms of data input sequences or camera speeds is also presented. The method demonstrates a capacity to scale, as the results show a capability to process over 50 NDT cells per millisecond. Additionally, an extension of the method's applicability to various sensor types beyond RGB-D and 3D point clouds was demonstrated, as the method successfully localizes 2D image descriptors across previous studies using the same dataset. Lastly, an extension of the method's performance in an underground environment was presented, demonstrating a capability to perform place recognition in this unstructured and challenging environment. The method demonstrated a performance consistency in all underground sequences with a maximum ko number of 12. Interestingly, an extension of the method's performance in an environment with a significant overlap between query and database poses was presented, as the method demonstrated a performance consistency in all sequences with a maximum ko value of 4. The method outperformed existing benchmarks by a large margin and showed a significant potential for use in 3D place recognition applications. The method performed optimally in all datasets and was capable of real-time processing. The code for this method has been made publicly available for the community at https://github.com/Dr-Lozupone/NDT-Transformer. The method's processing capabilities have been tested using PyTorch 1.7.0, OpenCV 4.1.0, and PCD 1.2.0. The method's execution environment is as follows: - CPU: 2.01 GHz with 16 cores - RAM: 32 GB

Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of resting-state functional MRI connectivity in predicting cognitive and psychiatric disorders. Although individual sites have contributed to this knowledge, research has yet to explore the benefits of combining data from multiple centers for connectivity analysis and predictive accuracy. In this study, we examined how data collaboration affects our understanding of brain connectivity and our ability to forecast disorders like Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia using resting-state functional MRI. Three datasets from the HCP, ABCD, and the ENIGMA-Alzheimer's and schizophrenia cohorts were utilized for this investigation. By applying the same preprocessing and correlation steps to data from multiple sites, we examined the impact of combining small datasets. In all cases, site-level analysis led to greater insights into brain connectivity and more precise disease prediction when compared to single-site studies. These findings emphasize the importance of data collaboration for improved cognitive and psychiatric research outcomes. When data collaboration tools were applied, regional connectivity analysis revealed greater consistency and accuracy. In the context of predictive accuracy, our models achieved better outcomes when predicting Alzheimer's disease risk in the ENIGMA-SDR cohort when data from multiple sites were combined. A significant correlation between functional and structural measures of the medial temporal lobe was observed, underscoring its role in predicting Alzheimer's disease. These findings have the potential to significantly contribute to the development of novel diagnostic tools for brain disorders and may lead to the development of new biomarkers following further validation. They also open new avenues for multi-site collaborative research in the neuroimaging field, potentially fostering future initiatives and programs. In terms of data sharing, our models and analysis have been made publicly available, along with preprocessing scripts and a participant t-score dataset for each study. We also offer access to a shared GitHub repository containing the data, analysis, and models from the ENIGMA-SDR cohorts, along with links to the individual site datasets. These resources will facilitate future research and data sharing, ultimately promoting an data-sharing culture. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language contact languages, particularly 
in socially media platforms. A major challenge in processing code-mixed texts 
arises from handling the intermingling of two distinct languages, often with 
different grammatical structures, at various levels of the sentence. To address 
this issue, a groundbreaking approach has proposed using positional 
encodings tied to the participating languages. Nevertheless, this technique necessitates 
predefined language knowledge, often difficult to obtain, and fails to adapt 
when the language contact scenario changes. In response to these limitations, our 
method proposes a new technique for generating positional encodings, based on 
switching points detection and analysis of monolingual texts' structural 
characteristics. When evaluated across multiple code-mixed datasets across 
various language pairs, our results demonstrate the efficacy and adaptability of 
this position encoding strategy. Furthermore, our positional encoding method 
outperforms previously proposed approaches, paving the way for further research 
on processing code-mixed texts autonomously without requiring prior knowledge 
of the participating languages. The experiments and associated materials are 
publicly accessible via the GitHub repository https://github.com/teo-mes/PESTO.

This paper presents an innovative method to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on map-based constraints to find the most suitable paths. However, traditional constraint-based planning methods are often impractical in real-world settings due to the enormous amount of computations required to account for numerous moving objects. In an attempt to overcome this limitation, we have devised a novel approach that leverages deep networks and geometric constraints to generate and represent spatial boundaries for navigation in the presence of dynamic obstacles. Our approach involves two key steps: Firstly, we employ a spatial constraints generator network to produce spatial boundaries that can be safely traversed, using the dynamic obstacles' geometries and a target velocity as input. Secondly, we integrate the generated constraints into a map to facilitate motion planning. Our results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art motion planning methods in finding effective paths around dynamic obstacles. Moreover, the generated constraints can be used across various scenarios and even across different velocities, thus exhibiting generalizability. Ultimately, this allows for the integration of our approach with deep network motion planners to further enhance their capabilities. One significant advantage of our method is that it can easily be extended to handle more complex and varied navigation tasks. The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the absence of these phases in the LiFeAs system makes it an ideal candidate to test the separate and combined effects of magnetism and nematicity on superconductivity. By manipulating the chemical composition of LiFeAs to simulate the conditions found in iron-based superconductors has become a common practice. This study presents an extensive investigation into the low-energy excitations and the nematic susceptibility of LiFeAs through a combination of inelastic neutron scattering measurements. The results reveal that LiFeAs does not exhibit a nematic phase and its nematic susceptibility is remarkably low compared to other FeSCs. This implies that, regardless of external pressure or chemical modification, the superconducting properties of LiFeAs remain unaffected by nematicity. Consequently, this work provides substantial evidence that the superconducting properties of LiFeAs are distinct from those found in iron-based superconductors at high pressure. Moreover, it challenges the notion that nematic order plays a vital role in the development of unconventional superconductivity in FeSCs. This research also paves the way for future investigations into the relationship between magnetism and superconductivity in LiFeAs. Ultimately, this enables a deeper understanding of the distinct mechanisms driving the two phases of FeSCs: those that develop nematicity before superconductivity, and those like LiFeAs where nematicity is virtually non-existent. This research also raises important implications for future studies on the separate and combined effects of magnetism and nematicity on superconductivity. Lastly, this work highlights the significance of comprehensive in-depth examinations of the low-energy excitations in LiFeAs through inelastic neutron scattering measurements. This research did not verify any scenario where nematicity and superconductivity are intertwined in LiFeAs through quantum phase fluctuations. By allowing an evolutionary algorithm to manage agent behavior and arrange particles, we find that small population sizes are sufficient to yield effective solutions in a relatively short period of time. Furthermore, our research reveals that an evolutionary algorithm can efficiently create multiple successful strategies simultaneously, which cannot be easily achieved using a random approach. We observed that these solutions exhibit robustness and versatility in that they continue to perform well under changes in environment conditions, such as varying temperatures. Ultimately, our study illustrates the potential for artificial life forms to devise innovative strategies for self-assembly that surpass what human designers can create on their own. We hope that our model simplifies the complex process of self-assembly and serves as a foundation for future research in this area. We explore the trade-offs between three methods: finding a single, versatile strategy versus many, specialized ones; controlling for biased outcomes versus ensuring fairness and impartiality; and the balance between strategy complexity and ease of adaptation. A novel algorithmic method for generating diverse strategies for self-assembly has been developed. We demonstrate that our approach successfully yields a diverse set of known self-assembly strategies as well as new, novel ones. The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, minimal spanning acycles in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular value by the zeta function. To confirm this connection, researchers investigated the minimum weight acycles in graphs and showed that the linear algebra-based method used to approximate the zeta function leads to the same value. This led to a significant finding that the linear algebra-based method accurately calculates the minimum weight acycles in large networks, a result that was previously inconclusive. By analyzing random networks, scientists discovered that the graph-based approximation converges slowly to the average acycle weight of the network under a particular condition, determined by the network's geometry. Interestingly, the time it takes for the approximation to reach its target value can be characterized using a specific mathematical equation, and the size of this time window increases as the network grows larger. Moreover, researchers found that the rate at which the network's geometry affects its weight is directly related to the network's topological properties. Finally, scientists studied how persistence graphs, which capture the structure of the network's acycle weights, change under different network conditions. These studies revealed that the alteration of a network can affect its acycle weights in different ways, such as the length of the acycles involved and whether the acycle weights increase or decrease in the altered network. Moreover, researchers found that the alteration of a network led to the appearance of new acycle weights in its persistence diagram, and the size of these new acycle weights increases as the network grows larger. Additionally, scientists classified the alteration of a network into two categories based on its topological properties and showed that the alteration leading to the appearance of the longest acycle weights tends to have the largest resulting acycle weights. Moreover, researchers found that the alteration leading to the appearance of the longest acycle weights tends to have the largest number of acycle weights in its persistence diagram. Overall, these results demonstrate that the linear algebra-based method accurately calculates the minimum weight acycles in graphs through approximation, and the alteration of a network's geometry affects its acycle weights by changing the length of the acycles involved. Moreover, these results reveal that the alteration leading to the appearance of the longest acycle weights tends to have the largest resulting acycle weights and the largest number of acycle weights in its persistence diagram. Finally, these results show that the alteration of a network leads to the appearance of the longest acycle weights on its persistence diagram, and the size of these acycle weights increases as the network grows larger.

This paper explores a common framework for securing distributed log-in systems using federated learning, which allows a central server to administer a global dataset and establish a common model shared among participating clients. Although the framework is designed with security in mind, we identified two vulnerabilities that enable a malicious client to infiltrate the system. The first attack involves guessing a user's ID, and after a successful guess, we show how the attacker can isolate and extract the user's private key from the local server and the client. The second attack involves infiltrating the client using a pre-installed root certificate, allowing the attacker to access the local server and the client's internal data, including the user's private key. Notably, these attacks are executed solely through the client's local server and the client itself, without requiring access to the central server or the network infrastructure. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose two countermeasures. The first counter-measure involves introducing a randomized delay in the central server's operation, making it difficult for an attacker to isolate the user's private key. The second counter-measure involves leveraging the client's local server's non-linear characteristics to conceal the user's private key from an attacker. Our research evaluated the effectiveness of these counter-measures using both simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating a substantial security improvement against both attacks. By applying our proposed counter-measures, we found the probability of success for the first attack to decrease from 100% to 0%, and the probability of success for the second attack decreased from 100% to 0%. The real-world implementation of our proposed counter-measures showed the user's private key to be secure against both attacks. The probability of success for the first attack was found to be 0%, and the probability of success for the second attack decreased to 0%. Our proposed counter-measures are currently being used in production to secure a distributed log-in system, specifically designed with these counter-measures in mind, and has successfully passed various security evaluations, most recently a penetration test conducted by a renowned cybersecurity firm. The research was supported by a grant from a leading tech company, specifically aimed at enhancing the security of distributed log-in systems. Long document retrieval has been a longstanding hurdle in both reading comprehension and information retrieval. Recent pre-training models have shown promise in addressing this challenge, particularly in the retrieval and ranking stages of long documents. Nonetheless, issues persist in the realm of long document ranking, such as the presence of noisy labels and the challenges posed by unbalanced sampling of long documents. In our research, we investigate these obstacles and develop a novel bag sampling strategy and group-wise loss function to circumvent them. The bag sampling method utilizes five randomly selected short passages from a long document as both a query and a positive example for the purposes of information retrieval, thereby accurately capturing the document's essential features. Furthermore, we introduce a group-wise loss function to rectify labeling noise in long documents. By applying the combination of pre-training and bag sampling methods with the introduction of a group-wise loss function, we significantly enhance the model's ranking performance on the MS MARCO dataset. Notably, our proposed model achieves a notable MRR score of 0.6508, thereby establishing a new state-of-the-art in long document ranking. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/Tongkete/Long-Ranking.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to enhance model performance under low-label scenarios. Nevertheless, a major issue arises when pseudo-labels generated by current methods contain little to no useful information for learning, primarily due to the reason that early pseudo-labels generated by the model during training are based on highly uncertain predictions. To address this challenge, we propose an informative pseudo-labeling technique for Graph Neural Networks with an initial supervision scheme that gradually increases in difficulty. During the training process, the model first learns to generate simple pseudo-labels for easy nodes, then adjusts to produce more complex pseudo-labels for difficult nodes. We also introduce a novel performance metric to evaluate the informative pseudo-labels generated by the model. To prevent negative impacts of negative pseudo-labels, we modify the cross-entropy loss to a directed loss function that exploits the intrinsic symmetry of graph structures. By integrating our supervising strategy and directed loss function, we significantly enhance the performance of Graph Neural Networks with an extremely limited number of labels. Experimental results validate that our method effectively improves the model's classification performance across various real-world datasets. The source code is available at https://github/Informed-GNN. The method we propose has the potential to contribute to the advancement of Graph Neural Networks under low-label conditions. Moreover, due to its versatile applicability, it can also be applied to other deep learning models dealing with semi-supervised node classification in graph data. Consequently, similar techniques can be applied to other graph-related deep learning models to improve their performance in low-label scenarios. We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence regularized with a constraint in the context of exponential families, and introduce an improved moment-matching algorithm, incorporating a proximal optimization step. Leveraging the information-geometric connection between Bregman divergences and Kullback-Leibler divergences, the proposed algorithm is equivalent to a Bregman proximal gradient method, offering the flexibility to apply geometric insights from the approximation while using black-box stochastic updates. Building on this perspective, we provide rigorous theoretical justifications, including proof of objective monotonicity, convergence to stationary points, and rates of convergence. These novel findings lead to the development of a flexible family of stochastic Bregman proximal gradient algorithms, each targeting different types of R\'enyi divergence and Kullback-Leibler divergence. To demonstrate the practical benefits of our methodological contributions, we perform comprehensive numerical assessments on widely-used benchmark problems, revealing that our algorithm consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, often by orders of magnitude. Notably, we identify a correlation between the algorithm's convergence rate and the magnitude of its step-size choice, providing a framework for informed step-size selection. These theoretical findings are grounded in the concept of prox-regularity, and we further explore the smoothness properties of the R\'enyi divergence, opening avenues for improving the algorithm's performance. Ultimately, the proposed algorithm's robustness is illustrated through its successful application on three benchmark datasets. The associated numerical tools are made publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, we expand upon the theoretical findings presented in this work, providing an equivalent analysis for the perspective optimization algorithm under a convexity assumption, which is itself a form of proximal optimization, requiring a linearly constrained perspective divergence to reach stationary points. Building upon the success of the Bregman proximal gradient method, we develop a perspective optimization algorithm capable of directly minimizing the R\'enyi divergence, circumventing the need for a convex combination. The algorithm's development is facilitated by applying the perspective transformation to an exponential family, effectively acting as an involution, which in turn allows for a reparameterization of the R\'enyi divergence that does not suffer from the same convexity issues as its r\'enyi divergence counterpart. Consequently, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for the perspective optimization algorithm to be equivalent to a monotone variational inequality, marking a key conceptual breakthrough in the field of optimization. Furthermore, we derive lower and upper bounded constraints on the perspective optimization

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved through a differential game approach. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovative 'Asynchronous Stochastic Gradient Descent with Selective Communication' method omits communication in SGD by storing gradient updates in local buffers and updates the solution only after accumulating a predetermined threshold of updates. This approach was successfully tested on a logistic regression task using real-world aircraft safety data and in conjunction with the C++ + UPC language combination. Performance measurements revealed that, on 8 UPC processes, ASGDRD achieved $2.4$ times faster convergence compared to vanilla SGD, while also significantly reducing communication traffic ($8.6$ times reduction) when considering the underlying hardware architecture. Nonetheless, the convergence speed of ASGDRD and SGD eventually converged as communication overhead became negligible in relation to CPU processing time. Therefore, ASGDRD can be viewed as a scalable communication-reduced variant of SGD that is suitable for hardware architectures requiring frequent synchronization. A demonstration video is available at the following URL: https://youtu.be/pb4H_4i7t9g. Moreover, the C++ implementation of the ASGDRD method has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/UPC-Barcelona-Dei/asgdrd. A thorough experimental analysis was also conducted by incorporating selective communication in SGD based on varying data quantity thresholds, which was found to be effectively predicted by a dynamic model that estimates communication overhead based on CPU processing time. Following this investigation, ASGDRD was further optimized by preloading local buffers with gradient updates during periods of active computation and storing them in a shared buffer location. This optimized variant successfully reduced the shared buffer size and minimized energy waste resulting from non-active load operations on hardware architectures featuring underutilized resources. Consequently, the final optimized ASGDRD method was shown to achieve $9.8$ times faster convergence speed compared to vanilla SGD on the aircraft dataset. Additionally, the C++ implementation of the optimized variant has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/UPC-Barcelona-Dei/asgdrd-opt. A thorough experimental analysis was conducted to assess the general applicability of the ASGDRD method across a wide range of data sizes, which led to the development and testing of an additional optimization strategy. The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it quicker and cheaper to produce fake content. To safeguard users against misinformation in the near future, distinguishing deep learning model-generated content will be essential. For this purpose, researchers have compiled a dataset consisting of human and artificially generated headlines and discovered that humans have difficulty identifying the fabricated headlines in a substantial majority of cases. On the other hand, the most effective automatic method employed in this context, specifically transformers, demonstrated impressive accuracy, successfully filtering out around 85.7% of the content produced by language models. Moreover, this method was able to explain its outcomes by pinpointing the parts of the input data where the human and artificial models diverged the most. Interestingly, when the text length was shortened, the automatic method's performance improved substantially. This study's conclusions and the developed dataset may have practical applications and facilitate the exploration of the relationship between a text's complexity and its programmable simplicity. Ultimately, researchers hope that the developed dataset and the results obtained can serve as a starting point for the creation of content verification tools.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, such as the Square Kilometer Array, will likely adopt a regular grid architecture to minimize construction costs. Despite the potential for large aperture distributions and traditional correlation schemes, current systems may struggle to process the vast data volumes. To address this challenge, we investigated the possibility of dividing the frequency band into smaller segments, correlating in-time data in a manner dependent on frequency, and then evenly distributing the data across all antennas to facilitate the use of traditional recording equipment. Our research reveals that this approach, known as the Spectral Domain Reordering Scheme, can scale calibration computations to $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ with the number of antennas $N$. Moreover, SDROS has the added benefit of reducing by an order of magnitude the quantity of baseline correction factors required. These factors can be utilized downstream in the data processing pipeline through multi-frequency synthesis, offset tracking, and other methods. Preliminary tests using baseline data from the Very Large Array have shown promising results, and further validation with simulated data from a $N=215$ element array demonstrates the feasibility of the SDROS scheme for large-scale, grid-based radio interferometers. Additionally, we found that calibrating the phase and amplitude of the correlated visibilities can be accomplished in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time, a significant improvement over conventional methods. To take full advantage of this advancement, we developed an innovative approach, the Track-based Synthesis Calibrator. TBSC, which leverages the unique characteristics of radio astronomy data to reduce the calibrator sizes across each time track to $\mathcal{O}(N/\sqrt{K})$, resulting in substantial time savings for the calibrator loop. Using simulated data from a $N=215$ element array at a frequency of $C/\{8, 2, 1\}$ MHz, we found the TBSC algorithm to be highly effective. Furthermore, the TBSC algorithm can operate in conjunction with existing data processing pathways, and we are currently investigating its compatibility with the SKA1 data processing architecture. In addition to these findings, we are exploring the feasibility of extending the TBSC algorithm to support the use of the timestream approach in conjunction with the SKA. This collaborative research aims to address the challenges associated with data processing at radio astronomy facilities. While researchers have applied generative adversarial networks and their variants to generate financial time series and assist in portfolio analysis, their methods are often too complex for practical use due to high computational requirements. To provide a more balanced solution, this paper introduces an autoencoding variant of the conditional generative adversarial network, which effectively generates financial time series and selects optimal portfolios, all while prioritizing forecast accuracy and efficiency. Experimental results demonstrating the superiority of the proposed solution over existing methods have been achieved using real-world data on the S&P 100 stocks index. Furthermore, this paper explores the application of this balance between market uncertainty and trend prediction in both generative model training and portfolio optimization. We demonstrate that a moderate level of balance (50:50) yields the most accurate predictions and the most diversified portfolios. Additionally, this paper highlights potential future research paths for this solution. You can access the source code at https://github.com/nghuydat/Autoencoding-Conditional-GAN. Furthermore, the result serves as a transition function from four to three dimensions,
and is applicable in the variable flavor number scheme (VFNS) at $O(\alpha_s^3)$.
This is particularly useful for heavy flavor contributions to parton distribution functions. 

The paper includes the extensive calculations required for
scattering amplitudes involving massive quarks off gluons in four-dimensional space-time.
These calculations involve advanced techniques such as massive loop expansion,
with applications to heavy flavor contributions to parton distribution functions.
The result is a significant advancement towards understanding heavy flavor contributions
at order $O(\alpha_s^3)$ in the VFNS for arbitrary $N$. 

The result was achieved through a combination of algebraic computations and series expansions,
with the latter used to control algebraic complications and handle the complex calculations.
The result was then expressed using generalized Lippmann-Schwinger scattering equations,
and the resulting expressions were simplified through the application of Casimir operators.
 

The result was finally expressed using a combination of Poincaré-Baltzman and Feynman hook integrals,
and the resulting expressions were compared with existing results for the unpolarized case. 

Using this result, we have shown that the resulting polarized massive operator
can be expressed as a sum of three-loop gluon scattering amplitudes, each controlled by a different $O(\alpha_s)$ term.
The resulting expression for $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ includes a combination of one-loop gluon scattering amplitudes,
a two-loop gluon scattering amplitude with a massive leg, and a two-loop gluon scattering amplitude with crossed legs.
Each of these terms has been evaluated and the resulting expressions have been collected and the resulting non-analytic terms have been identified. 

The result is a significant step towards a complete three-loop massive operator to the variable flavor number scheme,
and is an important contribution to the parton distribution function literature. 

The result was finally discussed in the context of the standard model and the resulting implications for heavy flavor contributions
at order $O(\alpha_s^3)$ in the standard model.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive other diseases, data is often collected using multiple measurements that span years, but the rapid progression of these diseases renders linear models suboptimal, resulting in poor performance. To address this challenge, this research proposes the use of natural cubic splines, a method more suited to rapidly changing distributions. Two models that employ natural cubic splines are formulated, one accounting for time-to-event data with proportional hazards assuming its endpoint follows a non-homogeneous Poisson process. The models' efficacy in analyzing data is demonstrated through simulation studies and real-world applications in two pivotal trials evaluating donepezil for Alzheimer's, highlighting the method's ability to capture both short- and long-term effects. When applied to actual data, the models produce compelling results, indicating donepezil has both early and late benefits in delaying Alzheimer's progression. Furthermore, the models offer a quantitative understanding of the treatment effects observed in the industry's repeated measure summaries. Specifically, in one donepezil trial, the analysis reveals a statistically significant improvement in cognitive function beyond what can be explained by placebo response effects, manifesting as a non-flat relationship over time. Overall, the natural cubic spline approach provides valuable insights into Alzheimer's progression in the context of donepezil treatment. Additionally, the research discusses potential extensions to the models, including the application of natural splines to analyze repeated measurements in the presence of missing data and the exploration of early, weakly informative baselines in the time-to-event part of the model, an aspect investigated through theoretical considerations and Monte Carlo simulations. Preliminary findings suggest a method that could shed light on the relationship between early improvements on trial endpoints and the ultimate benefit derived from treatment, an aspect of growing interest in the Alzheimer's and psychosis areas of investigation. The ideas presented in this dissertation are prospective avenues to analyze Alzheimer's and progressive disease data, aiming to capture the rapid progression characteristic of these conditions in the models' results. As such, they can be applied to a broader category of diseases. The relevant software and data resources for these methods are available at www.svsec.com.

A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways via optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Action-CSA is capable of sampling multiple reaction pathways without initial guesses and successfully captures both the most dominant pathway and a variety of alternative routes. Pathway diversity is maintained through a crossover operation, facilitating efficient exploration of the reaction landscape. Action-CSA is evaluated by identifying reaction pathways for alanine dipeptide and myoglobin appended with tetrahydrouran, demonstrating a strong correlation between optimized pathway costs and corresponding simulation costs via molecular dynamics. Moreover, Action-CSA identifies tight transition states at high precision, demonstrating its potential for targeted optimization of reaction pathways. Finally, Action-CSA is extended to explore the conformational space of peptides and myoglobin in order to identify the most dominant folding pathways for these complex systems. Optimized pathway costs are in good agreement with corresponding simulation costs via molecular dynamics. In particular, peptide pathways optimized by Action-CSA show a strong correlation with corresponding simulation costs and accurately predict the most dominant folding pathways. Moreover, optimized peptide pathways identify notable conformational structures during the folding process, in line with existing knowledge. It is anticipated that Action-CSA will find useful applications in exploring the conformational space of various biomolecules and understanding their behavior. In particular, this strategy may be useful for uncovering the reasons behind the formation of amyloid fibrils, rather than the native structure, by optimizing and animating the most dominant unfolding or reverse pathways from the amyloid structure to the native structure. Similarly, this strategy may be applied to investigate the degradation of drugs within the human body by optimizing and animating the most dominant degradation pathways. Lastly, Action-CSA may be extended to explore the reaction pathways for arbitrary systems not amenable to molecular dynamics simulations. Interestingly, such systems may include proteins denatured beyond equilibrium, proteins with chemical modifications not accounted for in the potential, or proteins where the target structure is unknown. By optimizing and animating the most dominant folding or denaturation pathways, Action-CSA could provide valuable insights to designers to create optimal versions of peptides, proteins, or related materials. Moreover, this strategy could facilitate the discovery of potential lead compounds via optimizing and animating the most dominant binding pathways from inactive compounds to specific targets. As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, researchers have focused on combating the widespread issue of hate speech online. This comprehensive approach, which we call the Interpretable Multi-Modal Hate Speech Dataset (IMMSHD), consists of 20,000 Twitter posts along with detailed modality-specific annotations, allowing for a deeper understanding of hate speech expression in various forms. Our study showcases the effectiveness of our approach through experimental results on publicly available datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models in precision and F1-score by significant margins (6.5% and 5.7% respectively). Based on these findings and the proposed framework's success in accurately classifying hate speech content on Twitter, we recommend that social media platforms adopt a multi-modal approach to hate speech detection and develop more comprehensive guidelines for users regarding hate speech usage on social media. Recent years have seen increasing interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
numerous approaches being explored. One area of research focuses on search-based
methods, generating potential repairs through syntactic analysis and systematic
exploration of feasible solutions. Conversely, we investigate an innovative
approach inspired by the concept of bugs and repairs from a adversarial
perspective. By utilizing deep learning architectures, specifically Generative
Adversarial Networks (GANs), we are able to produce repairs closely resembling
those generated by humans. An important aspect of this research is interacting
with a judge (human or tool) to determine the quality of the generated repair,
enabling us to refine the output and achieve satisfactory results without
presuming existing fixes. An evaluation on Defects4J and Ibardin links quality of
generated repairs to the difficulty of repair, demonstrating better outcomes
for harder programs. Additionally, we successfully apply this approach to a harder
dataset, showcasing its potential for widespread use in APR. Sources, data, and
code are made freely available. Overall, this research offers a fresh perspective
on APR and lays the groundwork for applying natural language techniques to code
repair. An important consideration emerges from this investigation - what does
this GAN consider 'difficult' repair? An exploration of potential biases within
the model indicates the possibility of natural language-based biases affecting the
model's perception of code repairs. Future research should delve deeper into
potential drawbacks and advantages of utilizing natural language-based techniques
in APR. Ultimately, we hope this work sparks further investigation into the use
of adversarial networks for APR. An expanded version of this material can be found
at https://github.com/robs16/adversarialpatch. An early version of this work was
presented at ICPC 2020 under the title 'Using Generative Adversarial Networks to

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a collection of interconnected rectangles, with each rectangle defined by paired rates of mutual information. While this formula is computationally challenging, it provides valuable insights into the nature of interference channels and their interconnections. To better understand its complexity, we examine the formula's behavior in specific, well-known interference channels, such as the Gaussian interference channel, X-channel, and isotropic interference channel, finding that in these instances, it accurately describes known capacity regions while also highlighting potential gaps in existing knowledge. Furthermore, we discuss how various interference relationships can lead to overlapping, separate, or shared capacity regions of individual users, as well as the formula's behavior in scenarios where users share a single capacity region. By analyzing a range of distributed and common message scenarios, we explore how the formula's complexity varies depending on these shared capacity regions and their geometric properties. Ultimately, we acknowledge that calculating this complex formula directly may be a computationally impractical solution for assessing the capacity region of interference channels in general. Consequently, we aim to establish constraints on this collection of mutual information quantities in future studies, with the goal of narrowing down the formula's complexity and making it a more practical tool for evaluating interference channels in general. By understanding the constraints on this collection, we hope to be able to identify the capacity region of interference channels consistently and reliably across a wide range of scenarios. Moreover, we aim to apply these constraints to assess degrees of freedom in interference channels with no information spectrum. This study marks an important step in this direction. While this work primarily focuses on interference channels in general, it also establishes a theoretical connection between this complex formula and the capacity region of interference channels with one-way and two-way memory, tying the capacity region of interference channels to the nature of information spectrum. By understanding the nature of information spectrum, we hope to be able to identify the capacity region of interference channels that possess memory. This study marks an important intermediate step in this direction. Consequently, it lays the groundwork for future studies on interference channels with memory. By understanding the nature of interference channels with memory, we hope to be able to identify the capacity region of interference channels that possess memory, common, and shared capacity regions, and to assess their complexity and variability. Ultimately, we hope to be able to identify the optimal coding strategies and algorithms for interference channels with memory.
