This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. It is particularly suitable for modelling median-based duration targets, making it a great option for datasets with a large number of training data entries. We provide a demonstration of this method's performance using the AMSET dataset, showing it is on par with state-of-the-art duration models in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, a non-parametric variant of this method is explored, enabled by the output probabilities being treated as non-normalised and median-normalised log-odds. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks suffer from efficient use of parameters, as subnetworks share features ineffectively due to convolutional weight ties. Current optimizations often compromise accuracy, and there's a lack of systematic features sharing frameworks in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)-based MIMO architectures. To resolve these issues, this research introduces an innovative feature sharing framework for MIMO architectures by systematically allocating weights between subnetworks. This proposal, termed the 'Multi-Inner-Layer' (MIL) method, allows subnetworks to exchange weights across layers, effectively mitigating shared feature inefficiencies. To evaluate the effectiveness of this proposal, two benchmark networks '2D-CNN-MIMO' and '1D-CNN-MIMO' were designed and modified to incorporate the MIL approach. Experimental results demonstrate that MIL outperforms competing baselines in terms of model efficiency and accuracy on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets. Furthermore, MIL is shown to enhance state-of-the-art MIMO models, highlighting its potential as a universal tool for improving all MIMO architectures. This project's code can be found at https://github.com/asharakeh/MIL-MIMO. The findings were published in IJCAI '23.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques. Specifically, this involves exploring collections of handwritten manuscripts and early printed materials. Unlike previous surveys focused predominantly on contemporary handwritings, this one delves into historical documents, investigating their varied layouts, scripts, and timekeeping systems. A primary focus of this research lies in providing an all-encompassing catalog of existing datasets, with the aim of identifying common challenges and opportunities within the field of historical document image analysis and leveraging machine learning methodologies. Ultimately, this study seeks to stimulate further research on historical document image analysis. Key areas of exploration include the exploration and explanation of dataset characteristics, an examination of the dominant algorithms utilized for label representation, dataset creation, and evaluation, as well as a deeper understanding of the techniques employed for historical document image analysis. A significant finding of this research is that, despite the abundance of document image analysis methods, there is currently no suitable evaluation toolkit to adapt to historical documents. Consequently, this study introduces a novel, flexible, and language-independent evaluation framework tailored to historical documents, addressing both transcription and layout analysis. A comparative analysis of this framework reveals its feasibility and effectiveness. Furthermore, this research provides valuable insights and suggestions for future work, including the exploration of additional label structures, dataset creation protocols, and descriptory metadata. A thorough discussion on the potential applications of this research is also provided. The study concludes by highlighting promising avenues for further investigation in the field of historical document image analysis. A total of 65 datasets were carefully curated for this survey, carefully evaluated in terms of dataset characteristics, and analyzed according to their descriptory metadata and evaluation methods. A total of 49 datasets were found to employ the Transcription Transformation Tool (TTC) for label representation, while 16 datasets utilized other label structures. Concerning dataset creation, 44 datasets relied on human annotation methods, 5 datasets adopted semi-automatic methods, and 16 datasets employed fully automatic methods for label generation. A total of 44 datasets were found to employ the recognition of text layout structures, 43 datasets involved handwritten text recognition, 38 datasets analyzed page layout structures, 32 datasets identified timekeeping systems, 28 datasets focused on layout analysis, 16 datasets identified section separators, and 11 datasets investigated table analysis. In terms of evaluation, the majority of datasets relied on the accuracy of individual character classifications, while some also considered the effectiveness of text layout structure recognition, layout structure recognition, and layout structure recognition for timekeeping systems

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, a common problem arises from the joint overdimensioning resulting from the desire to accommodate a large torque output at the expense of reduced precision. While employing more expensive "precision" robots offers a solution, this method proves impractical for tasks involving high-speed machining due to resulting increased idle time. In this research, a cost-efficient method is proposed to enhance the precision of "standard" industrial robots by improving the accuracy of their position sensors. By utilizing a new flatness-based control approach, a decentralized system is developed for one DOF using two additional position sensors, enabling improved precision in-line with high-speed machining requirements. Following a detailed explanation of the control principle, the method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a simulation-based study before the research was put into practice on a two-planetary-gear Dodge Robot. Results show position accuracy was increased from 0.1 mm to 0.02 mm when compared to the original value of 0.1 mm, demonstrating promising potential for applying this technology in "standard" industrial robots. In theory, this solution could be applied to multi-degree-of-freedom systems provided additional position sensors are incorporated for each additional DOF. Nevertheless, this would likely be prohibitively expensive for most applications. An additional challenge involves addressing potential dynamic influences on the overdimensioned joints, a challenge requiring a more detailed and complex analysis. In practice, the researchers observed a visible impact on the dynamic behavior for the tested robot. Importantly, the research revealed the position error was largely determined by the speed rather than acceleration, indicating potential for applying this technology in a variety of machining applications. In theory, the research suggests the position error could be reduced to as low as 0.5 mm with three additional position sensors. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, even when restricted to bipartite graphs. A parameterized complexity analysis was first conducted by Chen et al., who developed a 2^(O(k * log k)) algorithm. A query remained, however, until Watanabe considered the problem parameterized by the size of a resolving set and another graph property. This led to the inquiry as to whether the problem can be efficiently solved if the parameter is set to vertex cover and k. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods typically rely on a large dataset containing some inaccurately labeled images, known as label noise. There have been a number of studies investigating how to counteract label noise, but few of these focus on the specific type of label noise found in medical image classification, which arises from the incorrect assignment of labels to individual image pixels rather than the overall image. In response, we present a new method for countering this type of label noise using a mechanism called the label refurbishment mechanism (LRM). LRM exploits the uncertainty associated with each pixel in a convolutional neural network to correct the label noise by analyzing the distribution of pixel uncertainty across an image. LRM can be used on a range of deep learning architectures with minimal adjustments and has been proven to be effective through our experiments using the RSNA-2019 challenge dataset. Furthermore, we compared the performance of LRM with that of existing methods for countering label noise and found that it outperforms these methods on this specific type of label noise. The performance of LRM will also be improved further through the application of additional methods for improving the accuracy of image classification. In summary, we present a new method for countering the type of label noise found in medical image classification using a mechanism that exploits the uncertainty associated with each pixel in a convolutional neural network. The code and dataset used in our experiments, as well as further details on LRM, are available online at the following URL: https://github.com/ryanwangyj/label-refurbishment-mechanism. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations. By allowing the disconnection of clock mechanisms on a function-by-function basis, we find that these definitions become more readable and easier to understand. The proposed method is shown to be applicable in the creation of abstract data types in HOL, offering a distinct advantage over conventional methods. Furthermore, our technique can be applied even when proof language reasoning is already established, offering a behind-the-scenes method that may result in more concise and understandable proofs. Finally, through our evaluation, we determine the optimal degree of clock depth necessary for practical use. Although some degree of clock depth is always necessary, proof developers may achieve satisfactory results with a depth of one, making the presented method a valuable behind-the-scenes tool. Ultimately, our technique allows for the achievement of termination proofs that are largely unencumbered by the clock mechanism. This research was conducted with the HOL Light proof assistant. The proposed method's source code is publicly accessible on the author's GitHub page at https://github.com/leeceam/locked_definitions. The code was used to generate the examples presented in Section 6.3. Specifically, hol_defs_thesis.zip contains an exhaustive list of definitions considered within this thesis. These definitions encompass a range of non-terminating and terminating functions, as well as definitions utilizing the lock and key mechanism to enforce termination. The generation of these definitions, accompanying HOL Light proofs, was executed via a JSTrengths.max_lock_depth loop for various degrees of lock depth from 0 to 10. Within the repository, users may select definitions of a specified lock depth and functionality. The integration of an optimal degree of clock depth was achieved through an analysis of the utility of definitions at lock depths one and two, as detailed in Section 6.3.1. Utilising definitions of lock depth one may lead to termination proofs that average 9-100% faster when compared to definitions of lock depth two. This optimisation may be manually applied in existing proofs to enhance their efficiency. The results showed the existence of various phases: phases containing multiple Weyl nodes with surface Fermi arcs; a Chern insulating phase featuring gapless surface states despite bulk gapping; a unique phase combining gapped, topologically non-trivial bands with gapless Weyl nodes, connecting to a Chern insulating phase; and a new phase specifically emerging in the Hofstadter regime, characterized by broken time-reversal symmetry, long-range entanglement, and fractal anyon excitations. This time-reversal-broken phase, distinct in nature from previously reported time-reversal-symmetry-breaking phases, is set apart by its fractional excitations on links. Between April and July, 292 newspapers had reporters covering the COVID-19 pandemic. Their coverage was linked to COVID health statistics in the areas they served. The research identified patterns, including connections between the number of local news articles and COVID-19 cases and deaths, as well as disparities in coverage and its related health statistics. Notably, there was a notable U-shaped correlation between local news coverage and COVID-19 cases and deaths. This suggests that both a small number of articles and a large number have a positive correlation. The research identified areas with the highest COVID-19 cases and deaths as those with smaller numbers of local news sources. It also revealed significant disparities in COVID-19 cases and deaths among local news sources, focusing on racial and ethnic groups. Furthermore, the study found that local news coverage affecting minority groups was associated with higher COVID-19 cases and deaths. The researchers suggested that a potential pandemic misinformation index could explain these patterns. They posited that local news coverage serves not only to inform, which is associated with better health outcomes, but also to stimulate public discussion, which is linked to higher COVID-19 cases and deaths. The study concluded by highlighting the need for more research on the role of discussion in the spread of COVID-19 and the importance of a diverse news landscape for public health. It also emphasized that local news can be a valuable resource, but it must be accessible to a diverse audience. The research provided evidence that local news can shape public opinion while also influencing health outcomes, which are intertwined. Ultimately, the study called for policies that maintain a diverse news ecosystem by preserving and investing in local news for the public benefit. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Specifically, advanced integrators like the N-body integrators of Balsara and SPH integrators of Inutsuka include angular momentum conservation as a key attribute. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM), on the other other hand, is a crucial component of these advanced integrators and is essential for handling far-field interactions. For the sake of maintaining conservation capabilities, FMM must ensure that momentum conservation is upheld at the six-dof level. Research has revealed, however, that FMM typically fails to conserve angular momentum due to inaccuracies in integrating the linear and angular momentum equations. As a direct result, total mass and linear momentum also become susceptible to conservation failures. Our current project aims to rectify this by adjusting FMM to preserve both linear and angular momentum, resulting in co-designs of general and symmetric force fields. Furthermore, experimental outcomes have validated our method, enabling successful simulations of the isolated rotator test case and a merging compact binary scenario with accurately conserved angular momentum. As a direct consequence, this approach has enabled extended and trouble-free continuation of these complex simulations. Interestingly, our findings suggest that linear and angular momentum conservation are separable and can be distinguished through our general force field framework. Ultimately, our co-designed general force fields have the potential to improve precision in FMM integrators, while our specific symmetric models can minimize computational costs for symmetric problems like the merging compact binary test case. As such, our method serves as an expandable design pattern for SPH codes, compatible with numerous advanced integrators including N-body and SPH integrators. Moreover, our force field designs possess direct applicability to various integration schemes beyond FMM, including tree and self-avoiding algorithms. Research into integrating these parallel ideas could yield further co-designs and enhanced force field products. Lastly, future projects could effectively leverage our co-designed force fields to explore and simulate the merging compact binary test case and similar astrophysical processes with greater precision. We develop an efficient, low-cost technique for augmenting existing data in
entirely controlled settings, like laboratory tests or medical imaging, and
present a new framework based on this concept. By applying transformations
to data samples drawn from a teacher, our agent generates its own informative
examples. A key challenge arises from the teacher providing multiple
interpretations of the data, and our theoretical analysis shows that these
interpretations can be combined in a way that maximizes the information gained.
We provide the first theoretical justification for this approach by relating
the mutual information to the difference in entropy before and after receiving
the teacher's feedback. A thorough empirical evaluation confirms that our
method significantly boosts learning performance in scenarios with both high-
dimensional observations and multiple interpretations provided by the teacher. Furthermore, our findings indicate that our technique is highly resilient against
potential drawbacks, such as decreased data utility or adversarial entropies. We
conduct a detailed analysis of the parameters that influence information gain
and observe that our algorithm's performance aligns with theoretical expectations. Ultimately, we examine the effect of our approach on the agent's capacity to generalize
and discover that our method enhances its ability to do so, especially in scenarios
involving high-quality teachers. The code for our experiments is made available
at https://github.com/andreaborelli/data-augmentation-experts. A future work
section discusses potential directions for research has been added at the end.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
To tackle the challenge, a dataset was created by removing a substantial portion from the original dataset launched at ICDAR 2021, specifically instances containing only the numbers '0' or '1'.
Each evaluation was conducted twice using distinct evaluation methods: one by focusing on previously unseen characters and the other on characters from unseen contexts.
Notably, the winning approach involved using a standard, publicly available baseline model without taking steps to adapt or fine-tune it for the competition.
The outcome of the competition was characterized by the minimal separation gap observed between the top models and the model that had only learned to recognize the majority character ('0' and '1')), with only '0' appearing approximately 31% of the time in the removed portion.
The separation gap for '1' was around '0.65%, suggesting there was a greater challenge in distinguishing when the read text differed from the dominant character ('0').
The second set of evaluations, focusing on characters from unseen contexts, saw significantly larger results, with separation gaps reaching up to '57%, indicating a much greater challenge in the competition.
The winning approaches from the two evaluations shared some commonalities, specifically utilizing an encoder-decoder architecture, incorporating the model entered for the competition, and using data augmentation through transformations like crops and rotations.
Notably, the top-ranked methods for the second evaluation also incorporated additional techniques, such as using OCR ground truth for pre-training purposes.
The winning techniques and models used for the competition have been made publicly available for further analysis and research purposes. Future work may involve developing more effective models for the competition by incorporating additional data augmentation techniques and using transfer learning to leverage pre-trained models for the analysis. Additionally, to make the analysis more comprehensive, it would be beneficial to release the model's source code for the competition entered. 

The competition's analysis and findings were presented at the 16th International Conference on Document Analysis and Recognition (ICDAR 2022).  The data and model results were entered in the 2022 Interpretability in OCR track at ICDAR 2022, specifically for the previously seen and unseen character recognition categories. 

The competition's findings were further presented at the workshop on Reading and Understanding OCR Output (ROCO 2022).

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the link between their dynamic behaviors and geometric properties of the underlying spaces they're defined within. To address this gap, a numerical method was proposed for determining geodesic distances in Gaussian random field manifolds, involving two main components: deriving the underlying metric (a specific first-order matrix), and computing the necessary Christoffel symbols from the derived system. These calculations are further used to solve the resulting system of differential equations through iterative approaches, such as Runge-Kutta. When applied to different scenarios, this method demonstrated its capability to estimate distances while also uncovering intriguing results where reversed geodesic curves exhibited distinct patterns from the originals, hinting at possible irreversible geometric changes within moving references frames. This method was particularly demonstrated with the example of the Fisher-Kolmogorov equation, showing its broader applicability to other research fields. Furthermore, it has been suggested that the proposed geodesic curve reconstruction approach could be adapted for inverse problems, including detecting early cancer indicators. To achieve this, a systematic statistical analysis was conducted to assess how tumor probabilities transformed over geodesically separated regions, leading to a significant finding where minimal alterations in metric coefficients can result in geodesic curves with significantly distinct features. This ability could potentially be exploited for accurate tumor detection and diagnosis by manipulating or altering the underlying metrics. Moreover, it has been discovered that the Christoffel symbol's spatial structure may hold clues for understanding the underlying processes of the models in question. These findings, along with others, have been successfully applied to the study of the complex systems mentioned above. This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner (NFSP) for managing two-phase flow within diverse porous media.
Discrete forms of the Reynolds operator in the Navier-Stokes equations can lead
to ill-conditioning and slow convergence rates in numerical simulations, especially
when dealing with complex porous media. Proven effective in steady-state
calculations, the NFSP method has now been adapted for time-dependent scenarios.
Our team has investigated and compared two NFSP techniques, each employing a
finite element and implicit time-stepping method. Through our investigation, we
evaluated the NFSP's performance against more conventional approaches, such as
the Schur complement and implicit schemes, using examples of highly diverse
porous media. Our study shows that NFSP methods exhibit superior convergence
rates, comparable to implicit methods, while also being more efficient than
Schur-type preconditioners, especially in two-phase flow and porous media
applications. Based on our research, we estimate that NFSP methods can save 10% to
20% more computational time compared to Schur-type preconditioners. Our goal
is to facilitate the use of NFSP methods in future two-phase flow simulations.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities must coordinate their maintenance, but many systems within these cities are often isolated in their own databases, complicating efforts to schedule repairs and keep residents informed. The GUIDES platform aims to resolve these issues by providing users with unified access to a variety of data, employing modern microservices architecture and containerization for flexibility and scalability. The GUIDES web portal serves as the primary connection point between users and data, utilizing a BAE system to visualize and interact with various layers of city underground, while also disseminating essential information to residents through a tailored smartphone app. By successfully implementing GUIDES in Toronto, Canada, developers and city officials have obtained crucial insights into the process and are now able to evaluate its technical and societal impacts. The GUIDES source code and materials are freely available for adaptation and testing by other cities. The impact of the project's human element is examined through the results of a survey conducted among Toronto residents, revealing the significance of the platform's repair schedule information, a potential model for other cities to adapt and refine. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and applicability: methods capable of handling large numbers of qubits often assume error distributions, whereas more accurate methods applied to specific experiments require explicit measurement histograms, which become impractical with increasing qubit counts. To address this issue, we propose and validate a new MEM approach that iteratively corrects the probability distribution, allowing both scalability and applicability to be simultaneously improved. In experiments involving up to 32 qubits, our method significantly outperforms existing approaches by providing an improved overlap with exact simulations in the quantum variational circuit setting, specifically for the circuit to solve the transverse-field Ising model. At the same time, our method is able to achieve this without relying on assumptions about specific error distributions. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in applications requiring precise marginal probabilities, such as estimating energy expectations. Notably, the estimated error margins exhibited negligible dependence on the number of qubits. This property, combined with the ability to handle large numbers of qubits, makes our method an attractive option for variational quantum eigensolver applications. Overall, our work demonstrates the feasibility of scalable MEM without the need for assumed error distributions, thereby paving the way for the practical use of quantum computers in realistic simulations. Moreover, our research highlights the existence of an upper limit for the overlap achieved through the application of MEM. This finding enables the derivation of accurate estimates of the cost required to achieve a predetermined overlap threshold. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for the practical achievement of high-accuracy results in realistic simulations using quantum computers. An implementation of the proposed method in the PyTorch and PyTorch-LightQFT frameworks is made available for the purpose of facilitating future research. Analysis has been further enabled through the incorporation of the analysis package for quantitative assessment. When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to assume the role of a skilled craftsman, capable of executing tasks based solely on the direction given by the human operator. In order for the robot to successfully complete these tasks, it must understand the underlying goals of the human operator and not simply adhere to literal instructions. This requires the robot to possess a understanding of implicit norms that govern communication, permitting it to develop reliable expectations based on the information provided by the human operator. In our research, we have investigated the potential benefits of allowing the robot to express its own set of norms through data visualization on a shared control interface. In particular, we have found that visual indicators of robot assumptions can effectively express implicit norms and lead to more accurate and reliable interactions between the human and robot, as evidenced by a series of tasks where the robot's skills were assessed in the context of a pick-and-place operation. This effect persisted over time, even when the human operators involved in the study began to utilize the shared control interface in a more frequent manner. In addition to examining the dynamics of human-robot interaction, our research also highlights the significance of implicit communication norms within such systems, providing insight into how the robot's understanding of these norms can evolve based on the information provided by the human operator. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that by allowing the robot to express its own set of norms through visual indicators, as well as by enabling the human operator to view and assess these norms, we are able to create a more stable and predictable environment of shared autonomy. This is achieved by allowing the robot to safely and reliably assume a range of skills within the context of a autonomous system. In order to explore these concepts further, we have made our code available on GitHub at https://github.com/SJTU-KRL/SharedAutonomy. A video illustrating the research has also been uploaded to https://doi.org/10.17605/OSG/2022/673395/C7C8D. Furthermore, the research has also been published in the workshop "Foundations and Applications of Exceptional Motion (FAME 2022)" at the International Conference on Robotics and Automation. A copy of the research can also be obtained from https://www.dropbox.com/s/2m9m9m9m9m9m9m9/SharedAutonomy.pdf. The research team can also be contacted via email at krl201710200@sjtu.edu.cn. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, these systems struggle to accurately navigate unfamiliar environments, especially those with significant changes in geometry. A new map representation, called HiTMap, has been developed to address these challenges. By combining a local metric map with a global topological map, made up of areas and corresponding maps, HiTMap provides a higher level of stability and control over map representation. This leads to better navigation outcomes and reduced drifting in unfamiliar environments. A detailed description of HiTMap's components, including its state and navigation algorithms, is provided, along with a real-world testing validation on a self-driving cartograph platform in two challenging environments. The results show that HiTMap successfully navigates and cartographs the environments efficiently. Further analysis also confirms the benefits of HiTMap's hierarchical representation compared to a flat map representation in terms of both state estimation accuracy and robot navigation performance. Additionally, the code and data used in this research have been made publicly available to the community for advancement. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images from such data involves a complex calculation and an underdetermined system. Typically, low-quality images result due to absorption coefficients' uncertainty and measurement noise, which can be compounded by the use of low-fluence X-ray sensors, leading to data degradation. A novel image reconstruction model has been developed to address these challenges through data-enhancing weighted least squares, color-matching image reconstruction, and a self-regularization and data-consistency optimization process. By introducing an intermediate image and tailored weighted least squares, the model successfully improves the quality of noisy sensor data while accurately translating it to image data. Additionally, the model achieves image reconstruction through an intermediate image and data consistency-based optimization that applies CT data-specific constraints, thereby ensuring that the images comply with the CT data and are free of noise. This model has been successfully tested using simulated data on a range of challenges, including data from various polyenergetic sources. This model's source code and 3D/2D synthetic data have been made publicly available for further research and development. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate predictions, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as negative refractive index phenomena. The required nonlocality of electron distribution decreases as the gap narrows, in line with a study using a precise quantum theory approach, thereby highlighting the relevance of nonlocal electron behavior in this scenario. The distinction between these approaches becomes more pronounced at larger lengthscales, in contrast to short lengthscales where quantum fluctuation effects dominate. Furthermore, we illustrate that modifying a local response model to include a negative refractive index gap can produce misleading results regarding plasmon resonance, in contrast to a nonlocal description that yields a vanishing resonance frequency as the gap vanishes. Overall, our findings support the use of nonlocal electron behavior to achieve novel optical effects supported by quantum theory. The study's predictions could potentially be experimentally demonstrated with the advancement of nanofabrication techniques allowing for access to longer lengthscales. In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that enhanced results can be achieved when users also specify the relative significance of those terms. Although CNER bears some resemblance to related tasks like List Question Answering and Entity Disambiguation, it uniquely requires a comprehensive collection of entities rather than a curated list, making our user-studied approach to date unparalleled in the field. We subsequently introduce a new CNER dataset and a web-based interface to facilitate our experiments, aiming to contribute to the development of more effective human-student collaborations in CNER. The research findings will likely be valuable for other tasks involving large entity collections and user feedback. The research code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/lethuman/cner_userstudy. The research data can be accessed via https://ethanllep.github.io/cner_userstudy/. Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets, such a structure is particularly crucial, whether we're looking at the growth of a single variable or how interconnected different variables evolve over time. When working with longitudinal data, additional considerations come into play, including the relationships between successive measurements for individual subjects and how these are distributed across the data set. In this paper, researchers propose an abstract data model called Chronos to capture the time-based aspects of longitudinal data analysis. By doing so, Chronos facilitates the creation of interactive visualizations that make it possible for users to navigate complex time-based data. By allowing users to view individual subjects in relation to the broader data set, as well as exploring trends across multiple subjects, researchers can gain new insights into how the data has evolved over time. By providing an interactive framework for data exploration, users can discover new patterns and relationships that might go undetected in a static visualization. We showcase the potential of Chronos through a new interactive visualization that has been developed, allowing for dynamic displays of longitudinal data. By providing a comprehensive framework for analysis, researchers can unlock the full potential of longitudinal data analysis. The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, however due to diverse and heterogeneous data storage, significant challenges have hindered the application of machine learning methods. Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have begun addressing these challenges through the use of GNN models, but many of these models still struggle to handle the sheer scale and diversity of EHR data. In response, a novel heterogeneous GNN model called eGNN has been developed to effectively learn from diverse types of EHR data. By leveraging the power of mixed-hop message passing, eGNN enables the computation of node, hop-by-hop message aggregation, and global graph prediction, thereby enabling the extraction of diverse subgraph patterns at multiple scales. In testing scenarios, eGNN demonstrated the ability to outperform leading GNN models and feature-engineering methods on critical disease diagnosis tasks, offering potential benefits in the field of clinical research. With further research and validation required, eGNN could potentially become a valuable tool for the analysis and mining of EHR data. The study's source code has been made available to the public on GitHub. The results of the study show that eGNN performs well across a range of EHR datasets and diagnosis tasks. In particular, eGNN achieves high accuracy in predicting diabetes, deep vein thrombosis, and hypertension. The results of the study show that eGNN achieves an average AUC score of 0.810±0.017, 0.835±0.019, and 0.522±0.028 for diabetes, deep vein thrombosis, and hypertension diagnosis tasks respectively. In comparison, eGNN outperforms the baseline models across all evaluation metrics. The study reveals that the performance of eGNN largely depends on the selection of critical time intervals, sample sizes, and the number of message passing hops. By analyzing the inner workings of eGNN, the study reveals that the model's performance shows a growing trend with the increase in message passing hops. In addition to its technical contributions, the study sheds light on the importance of accurately diagnosing certain conditions at different ages, which could have a significant impact on the development of clinical policies and programs. Ultimately, the study provides new insights into the challenges and opportunities presented by EHR data. The result of the study indicates that the model can be extended to other types of healthcare applications such as hospital readmission prediction. Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy analysis, we obtain electronic images that depend on the spatial arrangement of the flexible surface's charges. We observe that the solvent effects cause thin electrolyte films to adhere to superfluid surfaces, reducing the apparent charge present, while increased ionic sizes weaken these adherence effects. A flexible surface's oscillations cause electrostatic forces that depend on the ionic sizes and the applied potential, leading to complex ion arrangements. We find two types of ion clusters - one at the boundary and the other extending beyond the flexible surface, with the latter's extent influenced by the electrolyte's properties and the ionic sizes. A higher applied potential causes increasing ion numbers in the electrolyte and the electrostatic double layer, with the latter's thickness dependent on the ionic sizes. We find that the solvent effects cause the ion numbers in the electrolyte to decrease, resulting in reduced electrostatic double layer thickness. The increased surface charge due to the solvent effects leads to increased ion clusters beyond the flexible surface, which may enhance flexural rigidity. The increased surface charge and reduced electrostatic double layer thickness could weaken the influence of the electrostatic forces on the oscillations of the flexible surface. The increased surface charge, reduced electrostatic forces, and decreased ion sizes, however, could also increase the flexibility. Consequently, we propose that the oscillations of the flexible surface depend on various factors such as the electrolyte's properties, ionic sizes, applied potential, and the presence of the solvent effects. A more detailed understanding of these factors requires further investigation. The observed behavior of the ion clusters could serve as a criterion for evaluating the presence of the solvent effects at the boundary of charged flexible materials. The shape of the electrostatic double layer, influenced by the electrolyte's properties and ionic sizes, could potentially distinguish pure charges on a flexible surface from charges influenced by the solvent effects. The increased surface charge due to the solvent effects, however, causes the electrostatic double layer to thin, which could weaken the flexibility. Consequently, we propose that the thickness of the electrostatic double layer and ion arrangements depend on the presence of the solvent effects and the ionic sizes. Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with well-established models like fastText and ELMo. To challenge the model with more complex text, we compared PURE's performance with experiments conducted on less formal Request For Information (RFI) documents. The fine-tuned BERT model achieved encouraging results on the PURE dataset, demonstrating superior performance on binary classification and text summarization tasks. Furthermore, we successfully applied the model to generate summaries of RFI documents as input for a Requirements Management Tool. Finally, we outline potential avenues for further investigation and present a related demo at https://puredemo.cs.arizona.edu.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of maintaining a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is implemented to simplify the problem, which is further solved using mathematical transformations and the Talbot's theorem to yield a set of optimal parameters. A numerical evaluation demonstrates the impact of system parameters on energy efficiency and reveals that the greatest energy savings can be achieved with a two-relay configuration rather than no relay or a single relay. Moreover, the optimization of scheduling and power allocation outperforms uniform allocation and scheduling. It is observed that the greatest energy savings can occur when all transmission powers are allocated to a single relay. A comparison with a multi-user diversity network coding scheme shows that the new coding scheme offers better energy efficiency with a smaller number of relays. Lastly, the optimization problem can be solved by first finding the optimal power allocation and then the optimal scheduling, which achieves the best possible energy efficiency while maintaining a target outage probability. Numerical results validate this claim and demonstrate that the quality of optimal schedules is largely dependent on the optimization problem's objective function, which measures energy efficiency under different system configurations. A special case of these results reveals that the optimal 1-st schedule has the highest energy efficiency among all possible schedules, which further confirms the significance of optimizing scheduling and power allocation to achieve better energy efficiency. A joint optimization of scheduling and power allocation is also addressed, which combines these two parameters to yield a set of optimal schedules with the highest energy efficiency. A numerical evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the new scheme in maintaining a target outage probability while achieving better energy efficiency than a range of alternative systems. It is observed that the optimal schedules have the highest energy efficiency among all possible schedules, which further confirms the benefits of optimizing scheduling and power allocation to achieve better energy efficiency. A final numerical comparison of energy efficiency and outage probability shows that the new scheme offers better energy efficiency than a range of alternative systems while maintaining a target outage probability. Theoretical models that rely on non-equilibrium Green's functions have been used to study magnetically impure metals for many years. Recent advancements, specifically in the Relativistic Multiple Orbits method, have allowed for accurate incorporation of Dirac-Fermi-liquid effects in heavy impurity systems. Recent experiments have discovered the absence of Yu-Shiba states in Mn dimer pairs on the Nb(110) surface. To explain these results, we investigated an Mn adatom and Mn dimer pairs on the Nb(110) surface using the Relativistic Multiple Orbits method. Our research revealed that the YS states in magnetic impurities are dominated by a single orbital type, specifically the d_x^2_y^2 one for Mn on the Nb(110) surface. Our calculations predicted that an Mn dimer with antiferromagnetic ordering would exhibit a gap in the YS state, supporting the experimentally observed lack of YS states in such systems. However, our research also found that in the case of a minigap YS state, it is not necessarily suppressed. These findings highlight the significance of incorporating relativistic effects, spin-orbit interactions, and d_j resolution in the study of YS states. They also emphasize the importance of incorporating density of states contributions from the host material into the calculation of the local density of states. Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for unstructured 3D scans. Yet, the limitations of traditional point cloud registration techniques become apparent in industrial applications involving complex, curved surfaces. Advances have enabled the registration of 3D scans with curved geometry using least-squares based methods. Recent research has proposed a Distributions Transform and Normalization (DTN) method, which provides an analytical solution and efficiently transforms 3D scan point clouds into normalized distributions. Subsequently, a registration method was developed by matching normalized distributions and resolving a non-linear problem. Notably, the DTN approach has the benefit of avoiding point-to-distribution matching, which can introduce significant biases. In this study, a deep learning-based framework was designed to extend the DTN approach to include multiple scans and utilize a local mean distribution, thereby reducing bias and improving accuracy. Furthermore, a novel bias metric was identified and quantified, revealing that the DTN method is susceptible to significant bias in certain industrial applications. Following an in-depth analysis of the DTN approach, the framework was successfully demonstrated with the results showing a 95% reduction in error on a dataset comprising over 2000 3D scans from the Airbus DS group's dataset. Notably, the DNN framework achieved this level of accuracy without requiring additional reference data or physics-based simulations. The results of this study indicate that the use of a DNN filter can yield high-accuracy results in the registration of 3D scans with minimal input from the user. Moreover, the DNN framework retains access to the intermediate analytical variables from the DTN decomposition, which reduces the training time and increases the speed and robustness of the process. The incorporation of a DNN filter has the added benefit of lowering registration errors, and the use of a diverse dataset in the training phase has the potential to expand the range of applications. The DNN filter developed in this study is currently being utilized in the latest release of the Open3D software framework. The research and outcomes presented here may lead to a range of potential software applications in the registration of 3D scans with curved geometry. Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure and large volumes of annotated data. In 
the context of massive satellite datasets, securing sufficient computational 
resources and annotated data can become financially and logistically burdensome. 
This research aims to circumvent these problems by developing a simplified, 
efficient solution for analyzing and extracting meaningful information from 
satellite images. Specifically, we present a groundbreaking, state-of-the-art 
edge detection technique utilizing Gabor filters in conjunction with an 
adaptive thresholding method. This innovative approach leverages Gabor filters 
to create distinct frequency components and apply thresholding along the 
confidence level to produce crisp, high-quality edges. We compare the proposed 
Gabor filter-based thresholding method with established techniques on a 
dataset consisting of varied satellite images and find that it surpasses others 
in terms of quality and performance. For instance, our approach achieves a 
edge detection accuracy of 94.88% on an image of Haar patterns and 84.79% on an 
image of Harpier Island, outperforming other techniques. For further details, the 
full paper can be accessed at the provided DOI link.'

Resonant excitation of inner shell electrons by x-ray absorption leads to a complex high-fluence dynamics of few-electron systems. The resulting non-linear x-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES) can be calculated through intricate quantum-mechanical approaches, but simpler analytical models are also sought after. A rate-based model proposed here effectively describes the time-evolving state populations of a system undergoing a two-level transition from its ground state. By applying this model to a realistic simulation of Fe${}^{+3.5}$ in a solid, its accuracy and its limitations are assessed. Although the model offers a relatively simple and reliable description of XANES dynamics at high fluences, its applicability to a broad range of inner shell systems remains to be seen. Further research is needed to broaden the model's scope, particularly for systems with multiple excitable states. A supplementary material contains the description of the model, its implementation, its results, and a comparison with the results of a quantum-mechanical simulation. The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments. Nonetheless, its dependence on raw baseband signal makes it vulnerable to malicious attacks on the transmission channel. This threat could be unleashed by an adversary with access to the network and the capability to generate deceitful radio signals. Our research introduces an innovative attack on AMC, based on the concepts of Generative Adversarial Networks, using real-world radio signal data to create classified confusion among the Deep Neural Network. This attack successfully forces the classifier to make incorrect decisions on 51.67% of samples, this accuracy threshold cannot be reached by conventional methods. Conversely, a resilient AMC system developed using a mixture Generative Adversarial Model can recover from the attack's classified confusion, restoring the system's accuracy to 97.74%. The proposed attack and solution have significant implications for communication security and will be crucial for the development of future communication systems. Our solution can be applied to a range of applications, including image and speech classification. It expands the boundaries of adversarial machine learning attacks and defensive techniques into the realm of wireless physical layer AMC. Our work presents a novel defensive technique for the first time, counteracting adversarial attacks on AMC by employing offensive techniques. Our research demonstrates that offensive and defensive techniques can coexist and engage in a perpetual struggle, ultimately contributing to the advancement of secure wireless systems. Our solution for surviving adversarial attacks on AMC has the potential to be applied to a broader range of applications, promoting secure and resilient wireless communications. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores. This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, thus rendering it unsuitable for comparison using conventional preference modeling. Instead, we consider employing contextual preference models, which depend on the query instance and utilize preference information across instances. Our study examines the fundamental properties of contextual preference models and the relationships between different models. Furthermore, we outline various algorithms for generating rankings under these contextual models and discuss their computational requirements. Additionally, we present a new ranking algorithm for non-contextual models and analyze its limitations compared to the existing methods. An empirical comparison of contextual and non-contextual models reveals that the former can produce more accurate rankings, albeit the best results might not be achieved through contextual approaches in all cases, providing insights into the design of effective preference models for set addition problems. Lastly, we highlight potential applications of contextual preference models and suggest areas for their further development. The obtained results have led to the development of a more advanced model, which utilizes a distribution-based query representation, resulting in better performance with lower computational demands. The resulting system enables users to obtain high-quality rankings for solutions of the Liar paradox. Furthermore, we present two new models that generalize the distribution-based model and explore the relationships among all models in the hierarchy. Our study achieves a comprehensive understanding of the properties and computational requirements of the models. The obtained results have been successfully applied to a preference learning method, which transfers knowledge across instances, leading to improved performance compared to non-contextual methods. The study also achieves state-of-the-art results on the Liar paradox dataset in terms of the quality of the obtained rankings. An implementation of the system is available at https://github.com/cosmokat/contextual-preference-models. The obtained results have been successfully applied to a preference modeling challenge. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached an Impenetrable level of opacity in their internal workings. Investigating such opacity entails a deep examination of CNNs to determine the knowledge they have acquired during the training process and how this knowledge is utilized in the output. Various studies have aimed to address this issue by proposing Visually-Driven Explanations (VDEs). Nevertheless, existing VDEs are plagued by a problem in that they fail to satisfy two essential criteria: visually-accuracy and semantically-relevance. The outcome is visually-incoherent and semantically-irrelevant images that are generated without consideration for the semantic context of the input image. In an attempt to resolve this issue, we suggest an innovative approach that combines filter attention, visual filter synchronization, and a reverse encoding scheme to generate Visually-Semantic Filters (V-SFs) naturally representing the semantic context of the input image. These V-SFs consist of filtered images where the visual content is synchronized with the semantic information, and the semantic relevance of each filter is automatically determined via a proposed relevance encoder. By applying backpropagation to this unified model, we obtain Visually-Semantic Explanations (VSEs) that not only accurately capture the visual content of CNNs but also attribute importance scores that are semantically relevant, obtained from joint training, from a proposed relevance encoder. The proposed VSEs naturally satisfy both visually-accuracy and semantically-relevance criteria. The VSEs' ability to accurately capture the semantic context of the input image has allowed us to study the knowledge that CNNs have acquired during the training process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed VSEs' attribute sub-modules can be used for general semantic classification tasks. The study was conducted on ImageNet, utilizing a subset of ImageNet-21k that is disjoint from the training set used for the CNNs. The findings reveal that the proposed VSEs achieve superior performance on various classification tasks when compared to the baseline models. The study's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghura/VSEs-for-CNNs. As for potential applications, the proposed VSEs' ability to accurately attribute importance scores to each filter of CNNs has allowed us to study the phenomenon of CNN visual bias. Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a strict filtering sequence, we successfully filter out unqualified workers before the final annotation task, ensuring that only experienced and proficient workers complete the final summarization task. By applying this refined recruitment process, we achieve an impressive 90% content relevance rate while maintaining a cost-efficient operating expense of $0.13 per summary. Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting robust visual and textual features through joint learning of pre-trained 3D transformers. Nevertheless, existing approaches are hindered in handling sequence lengths other than 64 by rolling or truncating, and also fail to effectively capture, mix, and pass on temporal clues from nearby video segments, diminish the contribution of adjacent frames, and neglect distant long-range dependencies. To address these issues, we present TS2-Net, a text-video retrieval framework that token shifts and selects using a pre-trained 3D transformer, achieving significant improvements over the current best method. We achieve this by breaking down the 3D transformer into two parts: one that captures nearby temporal clues by shifting tokens towards neighboring video frames, and another that selects and refines meaningful tokens from all inputs. We conduct an extensive set of experiments, and our findings indicate that token shifting and selection achieve complementary effects, ultimately contributing to enhanced retrieval accuracy. Moreover, TS2-Net allows for flexible input video lengths, and we demonstrate its capability to sustain state-of-the-art performance even with a substantial input video length of 128 frames. We test the effectiveness of TS2-Net on various video datasets, including MSR-VSGC, Multi-Video Retrieval, and VATEX, and present the repository containing our implementation at https://github.com/whwu2018/TS2-Net. Through thorough analysis, our results confirm the value of token shifting and selection in text-video retrieval. We hope this contribution will inspire the development of further novel techniques to facilitate learning from long video sequences. We also conduct an additional set of experiments by incorporating TS2-Net with the current best method, and our results indicate that the hybrid approach outperforms existing methods by a substantial margin on various video retrieval datasets. Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are explored.
For low dimensions, we examine the AdS/CFT method using massive Type IIA as its underlying string theory background.
In low dimensions, we utilize supersymmetric black holes in Anti-de Sitter space as the dual phase for conformal field theories.
For concretes, we discuss four specific examples:
Firstly, we consider a conformal field theory in two dimensions with a specific type of symmetry.
We use the AdS/CFT method to determine a particular aspect of this theory based on an existing study, and then compare it to the results obtained through computations in the dual black hole background.
 Secondly, we consider another conformal field theory in two dimensions with an alternative type of symmetry.
We use the AdS/CFT method to determine a different aspect of this theory based on an alternative study, and then compare it to the results obtained through computations in the dual black hole background.
Thirdly, we consider a conformal field theory in three dimensions and use the AdS/CFT method to investigate its behavior under a specific type of symmetry modification.
By computing a particular field in the dual black hole background, we establish a relationship between this field and the symmetry modification.
Lastly, we consider a conformal field theory in three dimensions with an alternative type of symmetry and calculate a specific aspect using the AdS/CFT method.
By comparing it to the results obtained through computations in the dual black hole background, we demonstrate that the compactification of the string theory to a specific space-time manifold is required for the correctness of the computational results in this case.

In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely depending on a well-suited kernel function. Traditionally, Gaussian Process researchers have either designed kernels from scratch, picked them from a predetermined list, or systematically searched for kernel compositions within pre-defined parameter spaces. This paper innovatively leverages Genetic-Programming, utilizing trees of fundamental mathematical expressions to represent kernel functions, thereby broadening the potential solutions, though also introducing new complexities. Our proposed method can successfully address these challenges and uncover kernel models accurately reflecting data properties. Empirically validated on real-world time-series extrapolation problems, this method surpassed state-of-the-art performance while decreasing kernel intricacy. Moreover, it discovered kernel models mirroring domain-specific knowledge, thereby facilitating interpreter analysis. As a result, this method provides valuable insights into structure formation within Gaussian Process models. Its source code is freely accessible at https://github.com/jaysmith123/GP-Genetic. Additionally, our experiments' data can be found at https://github.com/jaysmith123/GP-Genetic-Data. More notably, the space of possible kernel expressions is exponentially larger than the conventional Parameter-Tuning space, thus dramatically enhancing the potential solutions. Lastly, expression symmetries were difficult to incorporate in the search algorithm. muons from the beam line, resulting in beam-induced backgrounds (BIB). This
background interference will impact detector operation, leading to reduced
performance. Various studies at the International Muon Collider Working Group
have explored BIB at colliders. In this paper, we offer strategic approaches
aimed at minimizing BIB, based on findings from past research. We examine BIB
types, their intensity, and spatial distribution to develop optimized methods
for reducing background at muon colliders. We focus on two main categories: 
beam losses with low-velocity muons (in the accelerator or on the downstream
track) and beam losses with high-velocity muons (in-flight decays). Proposed
strategies include increasing the beam current to optimize low-velocity muon
density, fine-tuning accelerator and detector design to reduce in-flight
decay density along the beam line, and improving the beam focus to decrease
high-velocity muon density. We also outline the need for specialized software
to simulate BIB scenarios and the desired outcome. This investigation serves as

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing the most optimal configuration. Spartan offers a range of key advantages, including the capability to achieve both task-specific and pre-defined sparsity, the ability to train from pre-existing models with minimal modifications, and a detailed, easily interpretable sparsity pattern. Spartan's effectiveness is demonstrated on ImageNet with ResNet29 and the IMAGEN dataset with ViT-13, where it achieves significant improvements in sparsity while maintaining impressive performance on downstream tasks. Notably, Spartan achieves comparable results to hard sparsification on ImageNet, and substantial performance gains on IMAGEN while surpassing other methods in adversarial robustness. Spartan's full code is publicly available on GitHub. This research is supported by the Office of Naval Research and the ARO Grant. A detailed explanation of the research can be found at spartan.csail.mit.edu. The research is carried out in collaboration with Ted Xiao, Anurag Nanduri, and Stephen Wenink at MIT-CSAIL. 

Key Research Outcomes:

1. Introduce a unique method, Spartan, for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity.
2. Achieve state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet using ResNet29 and on IMAGEN using ViT-13.
3. Obtain sparsity patterns that are comparable to task-specific models and adversarial robustness.
4. Obtain significant performance improvements while maintaining task-specific sparsity.
5. Obtain improved generalization performance while maintaining task-specific sparsity.

The research provides the first analysis of the generalization of neural networks with pre-defined sparsity and demonstrates the first method to achieve adversarial robustness through predefined sparsity. 

The research provides essential insights for analyzing the trade-off between sparsity and performance, for understanding the differences between task-specific and pre-defined sparsity, and for understanding the generalization behavior of neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. 

The research provides the first empirical study of the cost of adversarial robustness through pre-defined sparsity. 

The research provides the first analysis of the accuracy of approximated sparsity patterns and of the cost of adversarial robustness achieved by Spartan. 

The research provides the first insight into the importance of accurately approximating the sparsity pattern for achieving adversarial robustness.

The impact of the Tan-Popescu Rieffel parameter, $K$, on the contact density, $\bar{\kappa}$, of a colliding superradiant Bose gas in an external potential near a disorder-ragged wall has been investigated. Utilizing both the diffusion approximation and a scaling approximation for this system allows us to demonstrate how the contact density is affected by $K$ and the width of the potential barrier relative to the healing length, $\xi/a$. In the collisional regime characterized by $K\gg 1$, the contact density increases with $\xi^2$ when the imaginary part of the wave function vanishes, yet it decreases in the weak interaction regime with $K\ll 1$ for a given $\xi/a$. Our results also reveal the importance of Pauli blocking in the momentum distribution near $2m\xi/a$ for $K\ll 1$, which is unobservable in the collisional regime. Our predictions can be verified using momentum-resolved Brillouin spectroscopy. This research may pave the way for studying other unusual states of matter such as supersolid Fermi gas. For $K\ll 1$, similarities with the momentum distribution of a one-dimensional gas have also been identified. In the collisional regime, the predictions of our model are compared to simulations using a boundary-element method. In the weak interaction case, comparisons are made with the results of a zero-temperature density functional theory. Importantly, our research highlights the emergence of a new phenomenon - Pauli blocking - in a simple system, which has far-reaching implications. It also encourages the application of quantum hydrodynamics to simulate the behavior of highly excited states of matter. Furthermore, our study of the momentum distribution near $2m\xi/a$ points out the need for a density-dependent effective mass in density functional theory for describing the system. This discovery may lead to the development of new methods for accurately describing the behavior of dilute Bose and Fermi gases in the presence of spatial inhomogeneities. It also provides valuable insights into the behavior of superfluids at various length scales, including the microscopic length of the healing length and the macroscopic length of the potential barrier. Importantly, our research demonstrates that a new form of quantum phenomenon, Pauli blocking, can arise in a system of non-interacting particles if it experiences a sudden change in density. This phenomenon can be used to identify and study unusual states of matter, including supersolids through a supersolid-Fermi gas correspondence

To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing communication costs when decomposing tensors. A novel, randomized method for a tensor's singular value decomposition (SVD) is introduced in this paper, an alternative to the supergradient-type methods that replay data multiple times. Instead, this approach requires fewer passes through the data by generating approximate eigenvalues and vectors (V) from a single pass of tensor-matrix multiplication (T-Mat), followed by a series of passes that utilize matrix-power computations. This approach builds upon a randomized algorithm for the SVD of a matrix introduced by Yin et al. An efficient, randomized method for the Tucker SVD (T-SVD) is derived by combining the randomized SVD for matrices with the tensor tensor power (T-POWER) algorithm developed by Beyer et al. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated by expanding the randomized SVD for matrices to the rank-1 tensor SVD (R1T-SVD) and then deriving the T-SVD as a sequence of R1T-SVD operations. A series of experiments illustrates that this algorithm is effective for a broad range of tensor decompositions and matrix-matrix multiplications. Notably, for a matrix size of 10 million, this algorithm requires roughly 30-40 passes to achieve a high level of approximation accuracy (90%). The supporting code for this research is available at: https://github.com/krishnan-krish/tensor_svd_randomized. An evaluation of the performance of this algorithm on the TACC Stampede2 cluster reveals that it is well-suited for modern, distributed computing environments. In fact, for a decomposition of a 1 billion element matrix (rank 1,2,3) with 10 million elements per matrix, this algorithm requires roughly 33-45 passes to achieve a high level of accuracy (90%), and approximately 2-3 seconds per pass on the TACC Stampede2 cluster. Importantly, this algorithm outperforms the randomized tensor SVD developed by Gleich et al. in terms of efficiency for a broad range of matrix sizes. Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization, but this approach struggles to accommodate dynamic behavior exhibited by real-world networks. These networks often undergo changes in their topological structure, feature evolution, and spreading dynamics over time. To capture such dynamics, researchers have proposed various techniques for embedding dynamic graphs over time. These methods face challenges related to modeling temporal changes, incorporating temporal characteristics, and adjusting to varying levels of granularity. To address these limitations, a comprehensive survey of dynamic graph embedding methods is provided, categorized by temporal considerations and analysis. An empirical study explores the state-of-the-art approaches, discussing their insights and limitations. Additionally, survey-based evaluations from over 80 studies provide valuable insights for future research directions. Ultimately, the report concludes by highlighting notable research avenues and challenges in this area. An accompanying repository is available at https://github.com/eyeconomics/DGEsurvey to replicate the empirical results.

Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be accurately maintained. These methods have made notable improvements in many areas but have failed to account for the broader range of similarity constraints. As a result, suboptimal metrics in the embedded space have been the outcome. The existing research into their performance with noisy labels is still limited. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel loss function known as Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL), which captures and incorporates the distinct class distributions in the embedded space. The experimental findings using five benchmark datasets validate that considering these class-specific similarities and differences is beneficial and provides more distinct differentiation between classes. Moreover, we introduce an open-source library called OpenMetric to facilitate the development of novel metric learning methods that are flexible and scalable. The library provides multiple embedding spaces and can be directly used for metric learning in popular deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow. The documentation for this library can be found at https://openmetric-fork.github.io/.
