In many countries, local contact tracing efforts were a key component of COVID-19 mitigation policies, as they involved resident volunteers in identifying and informing close contacts. Many countries, including England, relied on professional contact tracers for the majority of their tracing operations. Our research, which used data from England's COVID-19 contact tracing programme, explored the effectiveness of local tracing partnerships, where resident volunteers assisted professional contact tracers, to understand their impact on contact identification and case follow-up. We found mixed results, but our analysis revealed that local tracing partnerships were particularly beneficial in areas with higher volunteer engagement, as seen in the 'Test and Protect' system in Scotland. Our research concluded that the value of local tracing partnerships to the overall contact tracing effort was difficult to assess, as they primarily influenced case-specific outcomes based on the level of local engagement. Our findings also suggested that local engagement affected the timing and quality of case follow-up, which had implications for the operational strategy of a contact tracing programme, as even small numbers of local volunteers can enhance the programme's performance. Our results further showed that local volunteers can complement professional contact tracers, as the main constraint on the contact tracing process was not the availability of resources, but the inherent difficulty of identifying close contacts, which is beyond the scope of both local and professional contact tracers. Our analysis of the contact tracing process revealed that the identification of close contacts depends on various environmental factors, such as the density of population, the type of setting where individuals were exposed, the level of infection risk, whether the settings were indoors or outdoors, and whether the exposures occurred through aerosol transmission or through surface contamination. The latter factor was particularly significant for private homes and pubs, where local contact tracers identified a higher proportion of close contacts compared to other exposure settings. Similarly, the engagement of local volunteers in the 'Test and Protect' system in Scotland showed that the identification of close contacts in private homes was significantly higher compared to other exposure settings. Our analysis of the follow-up of cases further revealed that the follow-up of cases from outbreaks in private homes was significantly higher compared to other exposure settings. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's position and orientation directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position and orientation through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods against simulated data and real-world robot scenarios, where we observed that while direct prediction excelled in simulation, real-world cases demonstrated that relying solely on image information can be insufficient for calculating the camera's pose. Therefore, we recommend integrating artificial intelligence-based methods for calculating depth or segmentation maps into the process to enhance the accuracy of the camera's pose estimation. Overall, this research aimed to contribute to the understanding of whether and to what extent it is feasible to calibrate an eye-in-hand camera solely using a single image. While direct prediction achieved impressive results in simulation, the real-world application revealed limitations of solely relying on image information, necessitating further development to overcome these challenges. In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to various constraints that are challenging to formalize mathematically. For RL applications, it is crucial that agents can detect and adapt to these constraints to ensure safe decision-making. This study investigates a novel issue of inferring constraints from an existing agent's behaviors. By assuming agents exhibit logical behaviors and using a constraint representation based on logical formulas and sets, we design an inference method that identifies constraints an agent is likely to follow. This method is then applied to a range of subtasks, including a robot's exploration of a room to find a tool or an agent's skill learning with temporal constraints. A novel constraint inference framework is presented, utilizing a Bayesian approach to evaluate the agent's behaviors and constrain inference results. Experimental evaluation on existing and newly introduced environments demonstrates that our proposed approach effectively infers constraints an agent is likely to follow. For graphs with a given number of vertices and treewidth of order $O(n^{1/2-\epsilon})$, treewidth can be computed in $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/\log^k{m})$ time, where $m$ is the number of edges, using $O(n^{1+\epsilon}\log^{-k}{m})$ storage for some constant $\epsilon>0$ and integer $k$. This improves upon previous results with storage complexity similar to $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon}\log^k{m})$. Furthermore, treewidth can also be computed in $O(n^{1+\epsilon}/\log^k{m})$ time with storage for some constant $\epsilon>0$ and integer $k$. This improves upon previous results with storage complexity similar to $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon}\log^k{m})$. Treewidth can also be computed in near-linear time $O(n)$ with storage complexity $O(n^{3/2+\epsilon}\log^k{m})$ for some constant $\epsilon>0$ and integer $k$. Building upon this result, we propose a new algorithm to compute vertex separators in near-linear time $O(n)$ with storage complexity $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon}\log^k{m})$ for some constant $\epsilon>0$ and integer $k$. The algorithm starts with an arbitrary ordering of vertices. It uses an algorithm inspired by Refined Splay Tree for maintaining vertex order. Then, it uses Algorithm 1 to maintain vertex separator. The algorithm terminates early if treewidth $\tau(G)$ is less than or equal to some integer $k$ for each vertex $v$ in the graph $G$. The algorithm iteratively removes the vertex with the smallest index until the treewidth $\tau(G)$ becomes the integer $k$. The algorithm returns the vertex order at this point. The analysis of the algorithm's running time and storage complexity starts with an analysis of the properties of the tree for maintaining vertex $\pi(v)$ in the ordering. The tree is a perfect binary tree where each node $u$ has at most two children $L$ and $R$. The algorithm then iteratively computes vertex $\pi(v)$ in the tree and updates the tree based on the choice of vertex $\pi(v)$. The algorithm terminates early if treewidth $\tau(G)$ is less than or equal to some integer $k$ for each vertex $v$ in the graph $G$.

One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training sets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. However, the models' predictive reliability remains uncertain. In our research, we have developed an approach to PINNs that provides a theoretical upper limit on their prediction errors. This error estimation method, which only requires access to PINNs and proposed integration and differentiation procedures, can be time-consuming but provides confidence in the models' predictions. To demonstrate the potential benefits of this method, we have successfully applied it to two complex problems: solving ordinary differential equations that model predator-prey dynamics, and approximating the one-dimensional heat equation. Our results show a theoretical upper limit on the errors made when predicting time series using the PINN models for both problems. Additionally, the methods developed in this research allow us to assess whether increases in model complexity result in more accurate predictions, which was not possible with PINNs on their own. Ultimately, the methods developed in this research overcome a major limitation of PINNs by providing a theoretical upper limit on their prediction errors. distinguish themselves from traditional linear bandits by handling complex action
sets while maintaining comparable regret rates. To achieve this, we introduced
a new technique for exploring mean-relevant subgroups within the actions and
established the derivation of this method from several established approaches.
Furthermore, we studied the statistical properties of the learned models and

estimations. Moreover, we demonstrated that our algorithm's improvement in

Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of currents representing separate valleys flow in parallel.  Despite this proposal, it has been argued that the actual physical mechanism behind it involves the orbital Hall effect instead.  By comparing spin and orbital angular momenta using Dirac fermion Lagrangians, it has been demonstrated that the valley Hall effect can be seen as a manifestation of the orbital Hall effect.  Applying this distinction to graphene with gaps, it has been concluded that the observed effects previously attributed to the valley Hall effect are more accurately described by the orbital Hall effect.  This effect has also been mathematically represented using Bloch vectors for both sublattice configurations of graphene, illustrating how orbital Berry phases lead to a flow in parallel and an accompanying anomalous Hall effect.  Furthermore, it has been explored how the orbital Hall effect appears to be preserved under various scenarios including interactions, spin-orbit coupling, external magnetic fields, stacking configurations, and gate induction.  Lastly, it has been hypothesized that the application of an elliptical magnetic field could serve as a means to directly observe the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene.  This distinction between the orbital and valley Hall effects has significant implications for gapped graphene, as it has been traditionally studied under the assumption that the latter is the primary effect in play.  As a result, it is anticipated that this distinction will influence current understanding and future research on gapped graphene.  This study has also set the stage for potential future investigation into the combination of the orbital Hall effect with other anomalous Nernst, magnetoplasmonic, Meissner, Meotti, Skon-Jackson, Righi, Rode, Josephson, de Haas-van Alphen, debye, Shubnikov, Shoenberg, de Haas, Hall, and other related effects in gapped graphene that have not yet been addressed within the context of the valley Hall effect.  This potential for discovery and research is anticipated to drive future investigation into the gapped graphene.  This study has also set the stage for exploration of related effects in other 2D materials beyond graphene.  This potential for discovery and research is anticipated to drive future investigation into the gapped 2D and 3D materials.  This study also set the stage for exploration of related effects in 3D materials with a net orbital magnetic moment.  This potential for discovery and research is anticipated to drive future investigation into the gapped 3D materials

In this study, we will employ reinforcement learning to develop a data poisoning threat on Graph Neural Networks by introducing the RPG, a node reward function designed for graph data poisoning. We will also utilize Deep Q-networks to train RPG's optimal parameters. The novelty of our work lies in adapting reinforcement learning to graph data poisoning and exploring GNNs on reinforcement learning problems. For validation purposes, we conducted experiments on various datasets including Facebook, Twitter, and Wikipedia to compare the effectiveness of our method against the state-of-the-art. The outcome of our research yields promising results, especially for node classification, whereas challenge persists in edge prediction. A novel approach described here utilizes photometric data from multiple catalogs to enhance the astrometric matching process, thereby increasing its accuracy. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured descriptions called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise millions of interconnected entries, necessitating innovative visualisation strategies to facilitate understanding and exploration. While circle diagrams effectively showcase hierarchical relationships, they struggle with illustrating complex non-hierarchical associations within densely structured ontologies. To address this limitation, this study introduces OntoPlot, a new visualisation system combining circular and linear elements to clearly depict both hierarchical and non-hierarchical connections between pairs of entities. A significant improvement over existing methods, OntoPlot is capable of graphically representing all associations between two entities, even when they share no hierarchical connections. In OntoPlot's central circle, dominant associations are illustrated, while subordinate connections are depicted in smaller circular segments shared among secondary associations. A prominent axis then indicates the direction and magnitude of each secondary association. To ensure OntoPlot's usability on large, complex ontologies, it is accompanied by a novel, efficient computation method for determining non-hierarchical connections, which employs a graph reduction technique to swiftly and memory-efficiently derive the dominant and secondary associations between pairs of entities. In OntoPlot's computation, a novel graph compression strategy is applied to ensure that the graph's structural properties are preserved. A comprehensive set of test cases, including the UMLS and Gene Ontology, validate the effectiveness of the new computation method and OntoPlot's usability on large, complex ontologies. Through expert evaluation and user testing, as well as additional visualisation strategies for showcasing temporal evolution and the distribution of non-hierarchical connections, OntoPlot's utility in exploring and navigating large, complex ontologies is confirmed. We introduce an innovative technique to bridge the domain gap between a trained speech model and untrained utterances, leveraging CycleGAN. Our two-cycle approach minimizes cycle-consistent loss, combining it with an auxiliary inter-domain loss for more accurate representations. This method is scalable to various cycle losses and can be applied to different loss functions. We compare its efficacy with alternative loss functions, such as maximum mutual information, and recent cycle loss implementations, including one-sided and self-similarity loss. Experimental results on the Switchboard and Fisher datasets reveal that the method significantly reduces word error rate (WER), achieving a 13% decrease in the case of the Switchboard dataset. Consequently, this domain adaptation technique enhances the performance of end-to-end automatic speech recognition models, particularly in low-resource settings. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework. This framework is formed by combining information from various senses, aiming to create the most precise, self-consistent description possible, consistent with the senses and the assumptions one has. When there is ambiguity, the theory predicts that individuals seek information to refine their understanding and that expectations influencing one's initial framework influence one's course of action. Despite its potential in understanding and explaining animal behavior, incorporating active inference theory into artificial systems poses significant computational hurdles.

In this research, we present the application of a novel, deep active inference algorithm to guide a mobile robot through unfamiliar environments. To address computational difficulties, we employed a dynamic neural network strategy. This study marks the first instance of using multi-agent active inference for the task of autonomous robot navigation. To evaluate the performance of the deep active inference model, we employed both simulated environments and real-world conditions. The results show that the robot successfully navigates the environment by adapting to uncertainty and changing expectations. This outcome has implications for the use of active inference in artificial systems and may contribute to a deeper understanding of the theory's potential as a tool for predicting and explaining animal behavior. The code used in this research is publicly available at https://github.com/alexklyosov/deep-active-inference-for-navigations. The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper sets out to dispute the prevailing notion that large transformer-based models are inherently superior to their smaller counterparts, particularly in the context of Automated Essay Scoring. By investigating the performance of different language models with varying sizes and efficiencies, this study aims to provide a clearer understanding of the relationship between model capacity, complexity, and accuracy in AES. Notably, this research reveals that incorporating an output filter – a lightweight transformer-based model – can enhance the overall evaluation while reducing the associated computational costs. Moreover, this study's analysis of the models' memory usage, training time, and accuracy on PEWS scores demonstrates that large models with identical architecture to the base model but double the size and complexity (18M parameters) exhibit average improvements of 4.4% and 3.9% on dev data before applying the output filter, respectively. Furthermore, it is found that these large models' average drop in accuracy when applied with an output filter is 0.04 and 0.09, respectively. This research also discovers that the error introduced by the larger model's increased capacity can be rectified by employing a subsequent output filter. Notably, this study's findings highlight the need for careful model selection based on the available computational resources, as the benefits of employing larger and more complex NLP models may not be proportionally reflected in their improved performance. Moreover, the outcomes of this research provide guidelines for determining the optimal model capacity and complexity for AES, taking into consideration the prevailing trade-off between model capacity and complexity and accuracy in Automated Essay Scoring. Interestingly, the study's outcomes show that the fusion of large transformer-based models with a subsequent output filter – a smaller and efficient model – can produce more accurate results compared to the individual performance of each model. Notably, the combination of the BART and FastText models exhibits the highest average PEWS score among all the experimented models on the HSdata. Ultimately, this research's findings pave the way for the development of a highly accurate, computationally efficient, and practical Automated Essay Scoring system. Moreover, the study's outcomes provide valuable insights into the optimal model capacity and complexity for AES

One of the most significant issues arising from pedestrian detection models revolves around accurately identifying true positives while minimizing false positives. When such models are applied in the real world, a large number of false positives can lead to issues in data re-identification and surveillance, resulting in a significant increase in computational requirements. In this paper, we present an innovative solution to tackle unsupervised false positive suppression for pedestrian detection by leveraging the characteristics of bounding boxes. Our proposed method generates high-quality boxes through a re-ranking process, forcing detectors to converge on a single box per individual. This approach can be effectively applied to any domain adaptation method and has been successfully tested on public datasets, showcasing its superiority over the existing suppression methods available. Further analysis of our method reveals that the convergence of boxes occurs through a process governed by Gaussian distribution, underscoring the importance of box representation in visual object detection. Our implementation of this method is available on the GitHub platform. Additionally, the associated demographic bias of such a method is examined in the latter part of this paper. Demographic bias refers to the phenomenon where certain individual groups are under-represented or mis-detected in the collected dataset. Our findings suggest that box representation may introduce additional biases in the detection task, leading to the under-detection of older adults. To address this issue, we present an innovative label propagation method focused on improving the representation of box attributes, thereby reducing demographic bias in pedestrian detection. As a result, our proposed methods have achieved an impressive suppression rate of over 80%, while maintaining a high true positive rate of approximately 90%. Our research highlights the significance of box representation in visual object detection and presents an innovative framework for addressing unsupervised false positive suppression and domain adaptation, ultimately leading to high-quality detection results. Importantly, our method addresses the long-standing issue of scale bias and demographic bias in such adaptation tasks. Our research enables a more accurate evaluation of existing suppression methods, revealing their limitations. Moreover, our proposed label propagation method facilitates a more in-depth analysis of the suppression task by addressing the issue of attribute bias. Ultimately, our proposed suppression method significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, while our analysis sheds light on the box representation and scale bias aspects of this task. Our implementation of these methods is available on the GitHub platform. Moreover, our research reveals that the demographic bias in such a method is confined to older adults and can be accurately identified through our analysis. Consequently, our proposed suppression method successfully eliminates an additional attribute bias in the detection task, thereby leading to high-quality detection results. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, participants have a greater propensity to identify errors with a late point of release. Moreover, variations in the viewer's vantage point and the trajectory of the ball influence the overall perception of realism. These research findings could potentially be utilized in the development of more realistic and engaging simulation techniques for virtual reality applications. These simulations can contribute to a more immersive and realistic experience in virtual simulations. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN has been designed, which leverages tree-structured decoding with syntactic connections. By generating one sentence at a time, Seq2DRNN translates sentence segments in a manner similar to traditional NMT systems, yet with an added layer of syntax-awareness. This new architecture also enables neural dependency parsing and joint syntax-aware NMT and parsing. Experimental results demonstrate that Seq2DRNN yields a 0.7 BLEU improvement on the English-to-German WMT dataset and a 1.1 f1 score improvement on the CoNLL 2007 dataset when compared to standard NMT systems. Moreover, Seq2DRNN outperforms a benchmark model that utilizes syntax-aware decoding by a 0.6 BLEU score in an English-to-German translation task. Additionally, the model's syntax-awareness enables neural parsing and sentence alignment capabilities. This provides an efficient solution for integrating syntax-awareness in NMT systems, which can also be used for other tasks such as sentence alignment in the grey area between NMT and neural parsing. Interestingly, the model's tree-structured attention patterns mirror the syntax of the target sentence, revealing a 2.8% improvement in coherence when comparing manual annotations with attention patterns generated by a human label. This new architecture also outperforms a benchmark model that uses syntax-aware decoding by a 6.2% coherence improvement in human-generated metrics. Finally, the model exhibits desirable properties, including a 6.8% decrease in irregular translations and a 2.7% decrease in meaningless phrases observed in the baseline model. These experimental outcomes strongly indicate the value of incorporating syntax-awareness in NMT systems. The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture provides a versatile foundation for joint syntax-aware NMT and parsing tasks and yields notable improvements in coherence, which is in line with prior findings on neural parsing. The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account dynamic molecular structures and temperature effects. To address this need, our project developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP), a comprehensive database of temperature-dependent binding energy distributions that can be accessed for free at http://beep.astrophysik..uni-goettingen.de/. BEEP's database contains binding energy values for 375 different molecular pairs based on 161 distinct host-guest molecules, facilitating easy exploration by astrochemistry related categories. BEEP's database provides tailored binding energy values for specific applications and is intended to support research in the fields of extrasolar planetary systems, comets, and interstellar clouds by making cumulative binding energy values available to the astrochemical community. BEEP's platform is maintained at http://beep.astrophysik.uni-goettingen.de/. BEEP. Furthermore, it is available via https://doi.org/10.1037/JAS001630 for the related paper. In this review, we will examine the relationship between binding energy distributions and desorption spectra, discussing how the energy distributions are used to generate energy distributions and the various techniques employed in BEEP to calculate these distributions. Additionally, we will highlight the importance of experimental validation and the need for more detailed analysis of interstellar ice samples. Finally, the paper will explore potential data and calculations to support astrochemical modeling, as well as future directions for BEEP.

The main goal of text classification is to assign a relevant category to a given text based on specific features. Yet, a major issue arises when the training data is imperfect and real-world influences like spam and cross-contamination of training sets with testing data (known as label-variant corruption) occur. Existing methods, including robust overfitting, break down when faced with increasing levels of corruption. To address this challenge, a new theoretical framework for the dynamics of symmetric Boolean functions is developed by using the concepts of Arnold transformations and the coordinates of despinning. Based on this theory, a novel approach to a universal transformation invariant is derived, which leads to a creation of a sybil variant. Furthermore, a classification procedure using the sybil variant is introduced and extensively tested. It consistently outperforms other classification procedures, including robust overfitting, in nearly all cases, with a significant margin. Moreover, the results show a smooth, continuous decline in accuracy as the level of corruption increases, which is in stark contrast to the existing methods. The research data and the source code are publicly available. The research findings were also presented at a seminar. Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to an unrelated target task. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these linear features. Interestingly, our results demonstrate that achieving these objectives depends on either collecting data from unrelated tasks (for feature extraction) or employing specialized unsupervised techniques (for adaptability), highlighting unique requirements that cannot be satisfied concurrently. Ultimately, our theoretical findings are then expanded to address the more complex issue of non-parametric regression with polynomial representations, a problem that was previously an unsolved challenge. This extended analysis confirms the critical role of sample size in learning these representations and highlights the inherent difficulties of the problem. Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data availability. Post-hoc techniques like quantization and distillation are being explored to make these models more efficient for both resource and computational reasons. This research compares the stability of these two methods when applied to a multilingual Transformer base model when training them on a mix of high and low resource languages. Notably, our findings show that distillation yields superior performance when the knowledge coming from more fluent languages does not overpower the signals from less fluent languages. Conversely, the application of quantization leads to significant performance losses in all scenarios investigated. Given these outcomes, it's suggested that distillation be used to develop low-resource MT models if knowledge from related languages with more resources can be incorporated. Nonetheless, the efficacy of this approach depends on the specific conditions and the knowledge being transferred. Therefore, it's recommended that iterative refinement of both the training procedures and the training data be part of a larger strategy to develop robust, low-resource MT models. This research aims to contribute towards creating a systematic approach to developing lightweight MT models adapted to low-resource languages and various levels of compression. The code used here has been made publicly available via GitHub. Additionally, our findings have been shared with the NLP research community via an accompanying paper that explores the dynamics of compression in NLP models in detail. Finally, the findings presented here serve as an essential preliminary step towards advancing knowledge in this field.

The Turan number for an hypergraph F is the smallest number of edges in an F-free hypergraph. This concept was first introduced by Turan in 1941 for graphs, and its extension to hypergraphs is due to Ahlswede and Katona in 1967. For almost 50 years, researchers have been searching for formulas to calculate this number, but so far none exist. A notable result in this area is the determination of the Turan number for a specific type of hypergraph, which involves calculating its Lagrangian density. This was an unsolved problem for 20 years, and we present the solution here. A notable feature of our result is that it demonstrates the Lagrangian density can be an irrational number. This paper presents two methods for calculating the Lagrangian density, as well as providing more insight into our method by comparing our results with other theoretical findings. Furthermore, our research contributes to a broader theorem that was first introduced by Baber for a specific type of hypergraph F, and our results validate the theorem. The implications of our research are that for certain types of hypergraph F, any F-free hypergraph must have edges whose density agrees with that of the hypergraph F. This means our results provide an almost complete characterization of F-free hypergraphs. A further benefit of our research is that it provides examples of hypergraphs that satisfy certain properties, and whose density cannot be further reduced. These results provide valuable insights for researchers in this area, and could potentially be used to further develop our understanding of these complex mathematical concepts. The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying rare medical conditions is restricted by substantial reliance on extensive datasets annotated by medical professionals. Given that creating such datasets is highly labor-intensive, it's essential to explore alternative approaches that minimize the need for annotated data. In this paper, we investigate the effect of combining data augmentations on reducing the required labelled data for pneumonia segmentation in chest X-rays. We discovered that a combination of augmentations, which primarily involves image rotation, significantly outperforms individual methods and can achieve competitive results with much fewer labelled images. Notably, our best outcome was an AUC score of 0.898, which was accomplished using a 1% labelled data subset compared to the full dataset. Moreover, our results demonstrate that augmentations are dataset-independent and effective not just in our setup but also in other similar studies. Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to the desired style and level of detail. This paper proposes a unified image captioning framework that excels across various domains and can effortlessly adapt to multiple captioning styles. We incorporate a flexible prompt learning system that enables the model to absorb data from multiple domains, ensuring its performance remains strong in each domain. Additionally, we optimize the prompts using dynamic vectors within a VaLid set to achieve the best results in each target domain. This vector approach allows us to reduce prompt dimensionality and decrease model size, resulting in better performance and fewer parameters overall. Through extensive evaluation, our model outshines existing state-of-the-art models in domain adaptation and style transfer, while qualitative evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of our prompts and Valids in guiding the model's performance. Ultimately, our model becomes the first controllable image captioning system capable of adapting to any domain and style. This work is available at: https://github.com/ParadeParade/CaptionControll. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely relying on causality, surprisingly overlook causality altogether. By incorporating ideas from theories of action and causation, this paper introduces a new definition of harm that takes into account the actions of agents and their causal relationships. The proposed definition is based on two types of harm - actual and potential harm - and it highlights the importance of identifying specific targets, outcomes, and timeframes in evaluating harm. Furthermore, this definition emphasizes the necessity of contrasting hypothetical scenarios with actual ones, leveraging the principles of counterfactual reasoning. By applying this definition to address examples of physical and psychological harm, as well as example challenges like driving on the left side of the road, this paper demonstrates its efficacy in addressing seemingly complex cases. The definition of harm also illuminates the connections and distinctions between related concepts such as causation, harm, endangerment, and enability. Ultimately, this paper concludes that defining harm in terms of causality is a necessary step towards developing normative theories surrounding autonomous systems and general harm theories. The paper thus fills a crucial conceptual gap while contributing to the development of coherent doctrines of responsibility and the law. 

This research has also explored other related topics including definitions of causation and endangerment and models of enablement, and it delves into the implications for normative theories surrounding general harm and the law regarding autonomous systems. The ultimate goal of this research is to establish a fundamental definition of harm that can inform and refine both philosophical theories and the existing legal frameworks concerning autonomous systems.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, such as the amplification of inaccuracies in speech transcription into translation outcomes. Furthermore, these methods require substantial data for the speech recognition system to be effective. Our study introduces zero-shot speech-to-text translation, a novel approach that learns a single, unified transformer model to convert spoken language into spoken language of a different type using a middle representation. This model can operate on any speech recognition language without needing data for that language. We test this method on a significant speech dataset and compare its outcomes to those of conventional approaches in terms of translation accuracy. Our experiments show that zero-shot speech-to-text translation can achieve comparable, sometimes superior, translation quality without needing data for the target language, although it demands significantly more training data for the middle representation than for the speech recognition system. We open-source this method to facilitate its advancement in the field of multilingual speech-to-text translation. With continuous training on intermediate representations for additional speech-to-text translation languages, our model holds promise as an efficient technique for obtaining good outcomes on languages with limited data. This problem has been understudied compared to the vast literature on algorithm development. By investing time and resources in these algorithmic efforts, we can break down barriers to domain knowledge integration and foster a more successful machine learning experience. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in X-ray CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge about the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a key technique called spine rectification, the vertebrae column can be effectively separated from surrounding tissues and the undistorted appearance of the spine can be obtained. Building upon spine rectification, the new method offers a novel identification approach based on anatomical continuity, which starts from the sacroiliac joint, where optimized vertebrae positions and corresponding disk spaces are generated in succession. By analyzing multi-slice voxel features along the corrected spine axis, the method accurately identifies the vertebrae. Extensive testing on a large number of CT datasets with different pathologies has shown that the proposed technique outperforms previous methods by a significant margin, with an impressive 98% accuracy in single vertebral body identification. The source code for this research has been made available. The research has been published in a leading medical image analysis journal, with related CT dataset and model resources accessible online. The method's accuracy was demonstrated in identifying 7 cervical vertebrae with the use of cervical spine X-ray CT images and radiotherapy treatment planning images. Moreover, the research has been successfully applied in a clinical environment for the diagnosis of various types of spine disorders and tumors. We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary mixed quantum state via the relative entropy. All entries of the closest separable state can be approximated with a precision of $\mathcal{O}(2^{d^2\epsilon})$, where $d$ represents the qubit number and $\epsilon$ is the precision. This algorithm's efficiency is further analyzed, revealing a polynomial relationship with precision, problem size, and number of quantum oracle calls, albeit with a large exponent. This relationship holds under the condition that the state has a relatively low von Neumann entropy. This algorithm's performance benefit stems from the fact that low-entropy states require fewer tensor components to accurately represent the state, thereby reducing computational complexity. Utilizing three well-known separability methods - the Nconjecture, the Paldous method, and the Jordan block method - we assess the algorithm's performance and observe the Nconjecture to yield the most polynomial computational complexity. Furthermore, we validate the VSV's performance using numerical simulations of smaller systems. Although the algorithm's complexity appears excessive for large systems due to the high polynomial exponent, it remains a valuable tool for investigating the separability problem and identifying potential performance optimization strategies. Furthermore, we demonstrate its applicability to broader state problems, exemplified by the identification of the closest separable state with a precision of $10^{-3}$ in a $6$-qubit state with $60\%$ entropy. The algorithm's computational challenge stems from the required precision exponent $\mathcal{O}(2^{3\epsilon})$ rather than the problem size. This computational challenge is likely a result of the algorithm's variational nature, where the trade-off between precision and computational complexity can be optimized. Future research should focus on optimizing the algorithm's performance parameters. The algorithm's source code can be accessed via https://github.com/krishsaikat92/VSV. The dual gradient flow, which involves a particular type of gradient flow, is explored for solving certain ill-posed problems within the context of Banach spaces. 
In this context, the regularized problem being solved is defined by the formula $J_{\alpha, A}(x, h) = (h - Ah)^2 + J(x)$. 
Assuming that $J$ is a convex function and that the operator $A$ is coercive, it is demonstrated that the dual gradient flow is strongly monotone and that it produces a stable solution for the problem.
An estimate of the stability is provided in the form of an inequality.
This theoretical framework is then applied to solve an inverse problems associated with the heat equation. 
In this specific context, the goal is to reconstruct an initial condition based on sensor data, which is then compared against a known reference solution obtained through analytical means. 
To validate the results of the reconstruction, a series of numerical experiments are performed using the XDE solver in COMSOL. 
To assess the performance of the proposed approach, a variety of metrics such as the mean, mean squared, and Cauchy mean squared distances are employed. 
It is observed that the proposed approach produces a stable and accurate solution for the problem, which is also resistant to noise.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results. The paper reveals that double field theory successfully codifies all three gravity theories in a manner consistent with established research methods. However, for two of the theories – Carrollian and string Newton-Cartan gravity – the corresponding action frameworks introduced in this paper differ from previously established research methods. Furthermore, this paper links the canonical data of these three gravity theories to their respective action frameworks, leveraging the framework of canonical quantum gravity. The paper concludes by creating action frameworks for new gravity theories in a manner that highlights the utility of double field theory as a unifying framework. The paper's findings have the potential to influence a range of fields, including quantum gravity, condensed matter, and various areas of string theory. In densely populated areas with outdoor bridge extensions, interference among them significantly impacts network performance. To mitigate this, we propose an algorithm that optimizes outdoor bridge placement. However, we also recognize the potential for indoor access points to contribute to this interference. To address this, our research focuses on developing a technique that identifies the optimal active bridge to contribute signal strength to each access point, with the goal of reducing interference within outdoor bridges and minimizing the need for unnecessary signal processing. This technique utilizes the IEEE 802.11k/v standard's feedback mechanisms to continuously monitor and adapt to changing network conditions, enabling fine-grained control over active bridge selection, and ultimately saving energy by reducing unnecessary bridge components. To achieve this, we first establish a model to allocate resources based on feedback mechanisms and assess the impact of interference on performance within outdoor bridges. An algorithm is then developed to identify the most optimal active bridge for each access point, taking into account a given access point's multiple signal sources. Notably, our approach operates without prior network planning or analysis, enabling instant decision-making upon activation or deactivation of bridge components. Evaluation results, conducted using a widely-used bridge architecture, demonstrate a significant 50% reduction in average packet delay and up to a 7-fold decrease in battery consumption, while maintaining throughputs comparable to a scenario with no interference. This substantial improvement in performance confirms the efficacy of our proposed technique in addressing outdoor bridge-related challenges. Moreover, our research highlights the value of leveraging IEEE 802.11k/v standards in achieving these results, and the feasibility of integrating these methods into production models for implementation and evaluation. A demonstration video is accessible at https://youtu.be/KHGlryyDcig. A related patent application has been filed, with the filing reference PCT/KR2020/017949. A preliminary version of this work was initially published as a paper at the 2020 IEEE WCNC. In contrast, the current manuscript significantly expands upon this previous work, integrating IEEE 802.11k/v standards and incorporating evaluation results obtained from IEEE 802.11ax technology, as well as network simulation results obtained from the ns-3 tool. Furthermore, the current manuscript incorporates additional performance metrics, such as throughputs and energy consumption, and the evaluation platform is expanded to incorporate the coexistence of multiple bridge components. Notably, the current manuscript was conducted solely by the author, whereas the previous patent was completed in collaboration with the team.
